hyBullets: KRAS gene is the answer on USMLE for the first gene mutated in colonic polyps, prior to progression to overt colon cancer.

topics.title: Autoimmune intestinal absorptive disorders
topics.summary: Intolerance to gluten (i.e., to gliadin proteins found in wheat, oats, rye, and barley; but not rice).

bullets: Intolerance to gluten (i.e., to gliadin proteins found in wheat, oats, rye, and barley; but not rice).

Causes type-IV hypersensitivity response where T cells attack the small intestinal villi, resulting in flattening of the villi and malabsorption. The biopsy/image is pass-level. Below, we have normal villi on the left, and flattening of villi in Celiac on the right.
D-xylose test is abnormal because the intestinal lining/architecture is abnormal (i.e., we have flattening of villi).
Increased risk of gastrointestinal T-cell lymphoma in Celiac. This is called enteropathy-associated T-Cell lymphoma (EATL).
Diagnosis is made via antibody screening, followed by duodenal biopsy as confirmatory.
Treatment of Celiac is simply with gluten-free diet.

hySections.heading: Milk protein allergy
bullets: Biggest risk factor is not being exclusively breastfed for the first 6 months of life.
Will present as blood in the stool in a child who they say is, e.g., 4 months old, who was started on formula 3 weeks ago.
Treatment is switching to hydrolyzed casein formula. Switching to soy-based formula is wrong answer. There is up to 50% crossover of allergy cases with kids who have milk- and soy-protein allergy.
Vignette can say kid was started on either a cow-milk or soy formula when symptoms started. It doesn’t matter. Just choose hydrolyzed casein as answer.

topics.title: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)
topics.summary: Don’t confuse with IBD. IBS is psychosomatic (i.e., psych-related) condition.

bullets: Don’t confuse with IBD. IBS is psychosomatic (i.e., psych-related) condition.
Classic vignette will be a woman 20s-40s with stress factors who usually has alternating diarrhea / constipation; can also present as bloating or cramping.
Key detail is that symptoms are relieved with bowel motions.
NBME assesses “smooth muscle hypersensitivity” as the answer for the mechanism for IBS.

Treatment for diarrhea-predominant IBS is loperamide, which is an opioid that causes constipation. USMLE will give vignette of IBS with diarrhea, and then the answer is just “mu-opioid receptor agonist.” Other HY GI motility scenarios

hySections.heading: Diabetes
bullets: Diabetic gastroparesis = ↓ peristalsis due to neuropathy of the GI tract.
Presents as GERD-like presentation in someone with Hx of advanced diabetes.

USMLE wants endoscopy first to rule-out physical obstruction. If endoscopy is negative, do gastric-emptying scintigraphy (aka gastric emptying scintigraphic assay) to confirm delayed gastric emptying.

Metoclopramide is used 1st for Tx. It is a prokinetic agent (i.e., ↑ peristalsis) and anti- emetic. It is a D2 antagonist but also an antagonist of serotonin 5HT3 and agonist of 5HT4 receptors. The effects on serotonin receptors ↑ gut peristalsis.
Erythromycin can also be used to agonize motilin receptors.
“2-week trial of PPI” is wrong answer. This is the answer for “regular GERD.” If the patient has GERD-like presentation with advanced diabetes, however, the Dx is diabetic gastroparesis, not GERD.
Neuropathy to the hypogastric nerves (sympathetic) causes severe diarrhea. This is because the sympathetic nerves are “anti-peristalsis,” so if we knock them out, we get too much peristalsis.

Neuropathy to the pelvic splanchnic nerves (parasympathetic) causes severe constipation. This is because the parasympathetic nerves are pro-peristalsis, so if we knock them out we get unopposed hypogastric.
In other words, diabetes + diarrhea → answer = hypogastric nerves are impaired.
Diabetes + constipation → answer = pelvic splanchnic nerves are impaired.

hySections.heading: Thyroid
bullets: Hypothyroidism can cause constipation.
Hyperthyroidism can cause diarrhea.
USMLE will give vignette of a thyroid condition with GI disturbance, and then the answer will just be “motility disorder.” This is same answer for diabetes.

hySections.heading: Supplements
bullets: Iron and Aluminum can cause constipation (“Aluminimum amount of feces.”)
Magnesium can cause diarrhea.

topics.title: Obgyn-related hepatic issues
topics.summary: HELLP syndrome = Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelet count.

hySections.heading: HELLP syndrome
bullets: HELLP syndrome = Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelet count.
Can occur as part of severe preeclampsia (HTN + proteinuria after 20 weeks of pregnancy).
Vignette will be pregnant woman >20 weeks of pregnancy where you see the platelets and Hb are low and LFTs are up. Not complicated.
Highest yield point for USMLE is you get schistocytes on a blood smear. USMLE is obsessed with this.
Causes of schistocytes on USMLE = HELLP syndrome, HUS, TTP, DIC, and mechanical heart valves. If you’re about to trip out, don’t worry, I talk about these conditions in the HY Heme PDF.

hySections.heading: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis Syndrome
bullets: Pelvic inflammatory disease (chlamydia or gonorrhea) that has extended to the liver capsule.
USMLE wants you to know this causes fibrin deposition on the liver due to the inflammatory process. This is similar to post-surgical adhesions, where inflammation leads to fibrin deposition.

In other words, they’ll show you some gross path specimen of a liver covered in yellow material + tell you a woman had severe pelvic inflammatory disease, and then the answer is just “fibrin.” Sounds odd, but I’m telling you how it’s tested.

topics.title: Heavy metal liver diseases
topics.summary: Inability to secrete copper into bile from the liver. Copper is normally excreted by the body via secretion into bi…

bullets: Inability to secrete copper into bile from the liver. Copper is normally excreted by the body via secretion into bile.
↑ urinary copper + ↓ serum ceruloplasmin (copper-binding protein in the blood; in the case of copper overload, body tries to minimize amount carried in blood).

Buzzy / pass-level detail is Keiser-Fleischer rings, which is copper deposited in the cornea of the eye. Vignette can give you what sounds like Wilson disease, and then the answer is “slit-lamp exam.”
Can cause ↑ LFTs with cirrhosis and Parkinsonism.
Copper deposits in basal ganglia, especially the putamen.
Parkinsonism in a young patient = Wilson until proven otherwise.
In old patient, Parkinsonism = Parkinson disease, normal pressure hydrocephalus, Lewy-body dementia, or progressive supranuclear palsy.
When a disease presents similarly to Parkinson disease but isn't, we call it a Parkinson-plus disorder. Wilson is an example of a Parkinson-plus disorder.
Treat with the copper chelator penicillamine.

topics.title: Hepatocellular Carcinoma & Liver Mass Pathology
topics.summary: USMLE loves gross images of these conditions.

bullets: USMLE loves gross images of these conditions.

HCC will present as one large solitary lesion, sometimes with mini surrounding satellite lesions. Notice how the HCC is one solitary lesion. HCC can also grow as a “confluent multinodular” type. But note how the cancer is still all relatively confined to one area. MRI shows satellite nodule of HCC that grows next to the larger, initial growth. In contrast, these are hepatic metastases. Notice how the lesions are everywhere. USMLE will show image like this, and then the answer will just be “colorectal carcinoma.” Another image of metastases. Not as obvious as the first image, but still you can see there are multiple lesions not confined to one location. Liver in relation to heart/kidney

Right heart failure (either due to cor pulmonale or CHF) can result in venous congestion within the liver. This can cause a characteristic mottled appearance on gross specimen known as “nutmeg liver.”

hySections.heading: Pulsatile liver
bullets: Just know this is an examination finding seen in tricuscpid regurg.
As I talked about in the HY Cardio PDF, the highest yield cause of tricuspid regurg on USMLE is pulmonary hypertension / cor pulmonale.

hySections.heading: Hepatorenal syndrome
bullets: Just know that in chronic liver disease, sometimes the kidneys can also fail.
This is supposedly due to ↓ blood flow in patients with cirrhosis and ascites.
Biopsy shows no abnormalities. That is probably the only notable point.

topics.title: Bowel ischemia
topics.summary: Patient with cardiovascular disease (CVD) + blood in the stool.

hySections.heading: Ischemic colitis
bullets: Patient with cardiovascular disease (CVD) + blood in the stool.
Caused by bleeding at ischemic ulcers at watershed areas in the colon (i.e., splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction).
Can occur randomly or due to inciting event like recent AAA surgery.
Diagnose with colonoscopy to visualize the ischemic ulcers.

hySections.heading: Chronic mesenteric ischemia
bullets: Patient with CVD + abdominal pain 1-2 hours after eating meals.
Caused by atherosclerosis of the SMA or IMA → consuming food ↑ oxygen demand of bowel → angina of bowel.

The timing of the pain in relation to meals sounds like duodenal ulcers, however instead of the vignette being a 29-year-old dude from Indonesia with H. pylori, it will be a 69-year-old dude with Hx of coronary artery bypass grafting, intermittent claudication, HTN, and diabetes.
Next best step is “mesenteric angiography” on USMLE.
USMLE wants “mesenteric angiography” as next best step.
I’ve never seen medications or endarterectomy as answers.

topics.title: Mandatory GI anatomy
topics.summary: L1 — - Supplies the midgut (2nd part of duodenum until 2/3 distal transverse colon). - What the USMLE will do is gi…

hySections.heading: SMA
bullets: L1 — - Supplies the midgut (2nd part of duodenum until 2/3 distal transverse colon). - What the USMLE will do is give vignette of SMA thrombosis in peripheral vascular disease, causing acute mesenteric ischemia, and then ask which structure is involved → answer is anything that is midgut (e.g., jejunum, ascending colon, etc.)

hySections.heading: IMA
bullets: L3 — - Supplies the hindgut (distal 1/3 of transverse colon until the rectum). - Same as for SMA, they’ll say there’s acute mesenteric ischemia of IMA and then ask for involved structure (e.g., descending colon). - USMLE will also ask cancer lymphatic/venous drainage, which follows the same distribution as arterial supply. For instance, they’ll say there’s a cancer of the descending colon, and the answer is “inferior mesenteric lymph nodes” or “inferior mesenteric vein.” Not complicated.

hySections.heading: Renal/gonadal arteries
bullets: L2 — - Gonadal arteries = testicular arteries in males and ovarian arteries in females.

hySections.heading: Aortic bifurcation
bullets: L4 — - Bifurcation of abdominal aorta into the common iliacs occurs as L4. - What USMLE will do is tell you a AAA repair is performed where a graft needs to be inserted between the aortic bifurcation and the renal arteries. Then they’ll ask blood supply to which structure will get compromised. So you need to say, “Well the bifurcation is at L4, and the renal arteries are at L2, so anything that’s IMA would get impaired since IMA is L3.” → answer = “descending colon.”

topics.title: Gram-negative rods
topics.summary: Enterotoxigenic E. coli causes traveler’s diarrhea.

hySections.heading: ETEC
bullets: Enterotoxigenic E. coli causes traveler’s diarrhea.
Will present as brown/green diarrhea in person who’s gone to Mexico or Middle East classically.
Heat-labile toxin ADP ribosylates adenylyl cyclase → ↑ cAMP.
Heat-stable toxin ADP ribosylates guanylyl cyclase → ↑ cGMP.

hySections.heading: EHEC
bullets: Enterohemorrhagic E. coli causes bloody diarrhea 1-3 days after consumption of beef.
Produces shiga-like toxin, which can cause hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS; triad of renal dysfunction, schistocytosis, and thrombocytopenia).

hySections.heading: Shigella
bullets: Bloody diarrhea 1-3 days after consumption of beef.
Also can cause HUS via shiga toxin.
Requires very few organisms to cause infection.
Main virulence is via its ability to invade, not the toxin itself.

Both shiga toxin of Shigella and shiga-like toxin of EHEC inhibit protein synthesis by cleaving the eukaryotic 60S ribosomal subunit. Step 1 is P/F now, although that’s known to be asked, so you can decide yourself whether you want to memorize the nonsense.

hySections.heading: Salmonella
bullets: Food poisoning is caused by Salmonella typhimurium and Salmonella enteritidis. The nomenclature has changed with time, but those names are acceptable.

Bloody diarrhea 1-3 days after infection from consuming poultry, or following exposure to eggs or reptiles (i.e., turtles, lizards, etc.). New NBME Q mentions bloody diarrhea in someone with a pet lizard.
Requires more organisms than Shigella to cause infection.

Salmonella typhi causes typhoid fever, which will be rose spots on the abdomen in a patient who’s “prostrated” (i.e., lying down in pain); can be either diarrhea or constipation. The reservoir for S. typhi is humans, not chickens/reptiles.
Salmonella can go latent in the gall bladder apparently.

hySections.heading: Vibrio
bullets: Vibrio cholerae (cholera) presents as “liters and liters” of rice-water stool in someone who went traveling to, e.g., Mexico. The way you can differentiate this from ETEC traveler’s diarrhea is that cholera is notably profusely high-volume.
Acquired fecal-oral (i.e., fecal-contaminated food/water).

Both ETEC and cholera vignettes can tell you the patient has 8-12 stools daily, so it’s not the # of stools that matters; it’s the emphasis on volume. Cholera causes death via severe dehydration and electrolyte disturbance.
Vibrio toxin has same MOA as ETEC heat-labile toxin (i.e., ↑ cAMP).
Tx is oral rehydration on USMLE; if patient has low BP or altered mental status (i.e., confusion/coma), IV hydration is done.

Vibrio parahemolyticus doesn’t cause profuse, watery diarrhea the same way cholera does. I’ve seen this organism asked once in an NBME vignette where the patient ate sushi (can be acquired from sushi and shellfish).

Vibrio vulnificus causes severe sepsis in half of patients. This is asked on offline NBME 19 where a dude went running on a beach and got sepsis, with no mention of consumption of food. But it’s apparently acquired from shellfish.

hySections.heading: Yersinia enterocolitica
bullets: Causes bloody diarrhea + either appendicitis-like (i.e., RLQ) pain or arthritis.
The RLQ pain is from mesenteric adenitis or terminal ileitis.
Toxin has same MOA as ETEC heat-stabile toxin (i.e., ↑ cGMP).

hySections.heading: Campylobacter jejuni
bullets: Bloody diarrhea 1-3 days after consumption of poultry.
Can cause Guillain-Barre syndrome (ascending paralysis + ↓ tendon reflexes + albuminocytologic dissociation in the CSF → Tx with IVIG + plasmapheresis).
Grows best at high temperatures (42 degrees).

hySections.heading: Bacillus cereus
bullets: Watery diarrhea and/or vomiting in patient who’s consumed reheated or fried rice. The process of heating/re-heating causes germination of spores.
Can also cause eye infections (weird, but on USMLE). They’ll say patient who’s had eye surgery + now has infection caused by gram(+) rod → will be only gram(+) rod listed.

hySections.heading: Clostridium perfringens
bullets: Watery/secretory diarrhea following consumption of poultry.
Causes gas gangrene (CO2 gas) due to production of a-toxin/phospholipase; presents as black skin / crepitus.
Can also cause emphysematous cholecystitis (air in gall bladder wall).

hySections.heading: Clostridium difficile
bullets: Diarrhea (pseudomembranous colitis) ~7-10 days after commencing oral antibiotics.
Antibiotics kill off normal bowel flora, allowing C. difficile to overgrow.
C. difficile is not normal flora, however. It is acquired via consumption of spores.
Can be watery or bloody diarrhea on NBME. Can also cause LLQ cramping (not RLQ as with Yersinia).
There is NBME Q where they say 28-year-old with LLQ cramping and bloody diarrhea 7 days after starting oral antibiotics → answer = C. diff; wrong answer is Yersinia.
USMLE doesn’t care which antibiotics cause it; can be any.
Diagnose with stool AB toxin test; stool culture is wrong answer.
Treat with oral vancomycin.

Vancomycin has poor oral bioavailability, so is usually given IV for things like endocarditis and meningitis. But for C. diff infection, that’s a good thing because we want it to stay within the GI tract.
Other fancy Abx like fidaxomicin, rifaximin, etc., I’ve never seen on NBME. More just masturbation around dumb factoids.

hyBullets: Enterotoxigenic E. coli causes traveler’s diarrhea.
Will present as brown/green diarrhea in person who’s gone to Mexico or Middle East classically.
Heat-labile toxin ADP ribosylates adenylyl cyclase → ↑ cAMP.
Heat-stable toxin ADP ribosylates guanylyl cyclase → ↑ cGMP.
Enterohemorrhagic E. coli causes bloody diarrhea 1-3 days after consumption of beef.
Produces shiga-like toxin, which can cause hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS; triad of renal dysfunction, schistocytosis, and thrombocytopenia).
Bloody diarrhea 1-3 days after consumption of beef.
Also can cause HUS via shiga toxin.
Requires very few organisms to cause infection.
Main virulence is via its ability to invade, not the toxin itself.

Both shiga toxin of Shigella and shiga-like toxin of EHEC inhibit protein synthesis by cleaving the eukaryotic 60S ribosomal subunit. Step 1 is P/F now, although that’s known to be asked, so you can decide yourself whether you want to memorize the nonsense.
Food poisoning is caused by Salmonella typhimurium and Salmonella enteritidis. The nomenclature has changed with time, but those names are acceptable.

Bloody diarrhea 1-3 days after infection from consuming poultry, or following exposure to eggs or reptiles (i.e., turtles, lizards, etc.). New NBME Q mentions bloody diarrhea in someone with a pet lizard.
Requires more organisms than Shigella to cause infection.

Salmonella typhi causes typhoid fever, which will be rose spots on the abdomen in a patient who’s “prostrated” (i.e., lying down in pain); can be either diarrhea or constipation. The reservoir for S. typhi is humans, not chickens/reptiles.
Salmonella can go latent in the gall bladder apparently.

Vibrio cholerae (cholera) presents as “liters and liters” of rice-water stool in someone who went traveling to, e.g., Mexico. The way you can differentiate this from ETEC traveler’s diarrhea is that cholera is notably profusely high-volume.
Acquired fecal-oral (i.e., fecal-contaminated food/water).

Both ETEC and cholera vignettes can tell you the patient has 8-12 stools daily, so it’s not the # of stools that matters; it’s the emphasis on volume. Cholera causes death via severe dehydration and electrolyte disturbance.
Vibrio toxin has same MOA as ETEC heat-labile toxin (i.e., ↑ cAMP).
Tx is oral rehydration on USMLE; if patient has low BP or altered mental status (i.e., confusion/coma), IV hydration is done.

Vibrio parahemolyticus doesn’t cause profuse, watery diarrhea the same way cholera does. I’ve seen this organism asked once in an NBME vignette where the patient ate sushi (can be acquired from sushi and shellfish).

Vibrio vulnificus causes severe sepsis in half of patients. This is asked on offline NBME 19 where a dude went running on a beach and got sepsis, with no mention of consumption of food. But it’s apparently acquired from shellfish.
Causes bloody diarrhea + either appendicitis-like (i.e., RLQ) pain or arthritis.
The RLQ pain is from mesenteric adenitis or terminal ileitis.
Toxin has same MOA as ETEC heat-stabile toxin (i.e., ↑ cGMP).
Bloody diarrhea 1-3 days after consumption of poultry.
Can cause Guillain-Barre syndrome (ascending paralysis + ↓ tendon reflexes + albuminocytologic dissociation in the CSF → Tx with IVIG + plasmapheresis).
Grows best at high temperatures (42 degrees).
Watery diarrhea and/or vomiting in patient who’s consumed reheated or fried rice. The process of heating/re-heating causes germination of spores.
Can also cause eye infections (weird, but on USMLE). They’ll say patient who’s had eye surgery + now has infection caused by gram(+) rod → will be only gram(+) rod listed.

Can also cause emphysematous cholecystitis (air in gall bladder wall).
Diarrhea (pseudomembranous colitis) ~7-10 days after commencing oral antibiotics.
Antibiotics kill off normal bowel flora, allowing C. difficile to overgrow.
C. difficile is not normal flora, however. It is acquired via consumption of spores.
Can be watery or bloody diarrhea on NBME. Can also cause LLQ cramping (not RLQ as with Yersinia).
There is NBME Q where they say 28-year-old with LLQ cramping and bloody diarrhea 7 days after starting oral antibiotics → answer = C. diff; wrong answer is Yersinia.

hySections.heading: Staph aureus
bullets: S. aureus pre-formed heat-stable toxin is acquired from two main sources on NBME: 1) various meats sitting under a heat lamp / out for long periods of time, e.g., at a buffet; 2) dairy products like creams, custards, potato salad.

Notably causes vomiting 1-6 hours after consumption. This is notable, as the symptoms occur rather quickly. Diarrhea, both watery and bloody, can occur, but is not mandatory. The main crux is the vomiting.

bullets: Causes Whipple disease, a GI malabsorptive syndrome where the patient can also get arthritis and renal and cardiac disease.

hySections.heading: Tropical sprue
bullets: Causes flattening of villi similar to Celiac, but considered infective/bacterial in origin. Literature says exact etiology not certain.
Answer on USMLE for patient living in tropical area with unknown malabsorptive disease, where you can easily eliminate the other answers.
Tx = tetracycline.

topics.title: GI viral infections
topics.summary: Most common cause of watery diarrhea in unvaccinated children < 5 years.

hySections.heading: Rotavirus
bullets: Most common cause of watery diarrhea in unvaccinated children < 5 years.
Vaccine normally given orally at 2, 4, and 6 months of age.
Double-stranded, segmented RNA (NBME asks it).
Wheel-shaped (also on NBME).

hySections.heading: Norwalk virus
bullets: Most common cause of watery diarrhea in adults and rotavirus-vaccinated children.
Cruise ships and business conferences are buzzy places to acquire (fecal-oral); basically any place with high density of people.
If the Q says a young child + family all have watery diarrhea, the answer is Norwalk, not Rota, since only the young child would get Rota, not the family also.

hySections.heading: Herpes
bullets: HSV1/2 causes herpes esophagitis → odynophagia + punched-out ulcers in esophagus.

hySections.heading: CMV
bullets: CMV esophagitis →odynophagia + linear (confluent) ulcers in esophagus.
CMV colitis → bleeding per rectum in AIDS patient with CD4 count <50.
CMV retinitis → blurry vision in HIV (or immunosuppressed) patient.
Most common organism transmitted via blood transfusions and organ transplants.
USMLE likes “intranuclear inclusions” or “intranuclear inclusion bodies” for CMV. This refers to the “owl eyes” that can be seen on histo.

topics.title: GI protozoal infections
topics.summary: A protozoan is a unicellular eukaryote.

bullets: A protozoan is a unicellular eukaryote.
Treat with metronidazole.
Iodoquinol kills intraluminal parasite.

Acquired via fresh water lakes / scuba diving. There is a Giardia NBME Q where they say a woman goes scuba diving in Mexico and then gets foul-smelling stools with bloating. Student says, “Wait but I thought Giardia was fresh water. If she went scuba diving in the ocean then how is that Giardia?” → People can go scuba diving in fresh water lakes too bro. Don’t know what to tell you.
Flagellated protozoan. USMLE wants you to know the images for both the cyst as well as the flagellated trophozoite. Cyst form of Giardia. Not dramatic. Trophozoite form of Giardia.
Tx = metronidazole.

hySections.heading: Entamoeba histolytica
bullets: Bloody diarrhea in person who went to Mexico.
Can cause “flask-shaped ulcers” in the small bowel and liver abscess.
Demonstrates “erythrophagocytosis,” where RBCs can be seen within it on LM.

hySections.heading: Cryptosporidium parvum
bullets: Watery diarrhea in person who went to Mexico.
Appears as acid-fast cysts (same stain as TB).
Self-limiting in immunocompetent persons → Tx = supportive care.
Chronic diarrhea in HIV → Tx = nitazoxanide.

hySections.heading: Giardia lamblia
bullets: Steatorrhea in person who went to Mexico.
Steatorrhea = bloating + extremely foul-smelling stool that floats.
The steatorrhea is due to Giardia causing malabsorptive diarrhea.

There is one NBME Q for Giardia where they say “foul-smelling watery diarrhea with bloating,” which is audacious, since 9 times out of 10 it is not described as watery. But the “bloating” and “foul-smelling” are consistent with steatorrhea in this context. Just letting you know it exists.

topics.title: GI parasitic (helminth) infections
topics.summary: USMLE wants you to know routes of acquisition for the nematodes (i.e., ingested or through feet, etc.).

bullets: USMLE wants you to know routes of acquisition for the nematodes (i.e., ingested or through feet, etc.).

You do not need to obsess over exactly which anti-helminthic agent treats which organism. Waste of time. What USMLE wants you to know is the big-picture concept that -bendazoles (i.e., mebendazole) and pyrantel pamoate are the two agents that treat nematodes primarily. -Bendazoles microtubules (tubulin) and pyrantel pamoate causes helminth paralysis.
Praziquantel is used for cestodes and trematodes. It causes helminth paralysis.
Albendazole is the odd one out that is used for neurocysticercosis (Taenia solium; cestode).
USMLE doesn’t tests diethylcarbamazine. Nematodes (roundworms)

hySections.heading: Ascaris lumbricoides
bullets: Ingested. Giant roundworm; causes intestinal obstruction. (Ascariasis)

hySections.heading: Enterobius vermicularis
bullets: Ingested. Causes perianal itching / (+) tape test in children. (Enterobiasis)

hySections.heading: Angiostrongylus
bullets: Ingested by eating raw slugs/snails. Causes eosinophilic meningitis.

hySections.heading: Trichinella spiralis
bullets: Ingested by eating pork/bear meat. Causes triad of fever, periorbital edema, and myalgias. (Trichinosis)

hySections.heading: Strongyloides stercoralis
bullets: Acquired through soil/one’s feet. Causes intestinal obstruction + pulmonary symptoms (apparently travels to lungs via blood, then travels up respiratory tree into esophagus, where it is swallowed).

hySections.heading: Hookworms
bullets: Acquired through soil/one’s feet. ”Hookworms” refers to Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus.
Cause microcytic anemia / ↓ hemoglobin due to sucking blood in GI tract.

topics.summary: Fish tapeworm. Nothing else you need to know.

hySections.heading: Diphyllobothrium latum
bullets: Fish tapeworm. Nothing else you need to know.

hySections.heading: Taenia solium
bullets: Pork tapeworm. Causes cysticercosis (muscle pain/cysts) + neurocysticercosis (“Swiss cheese” appearance of brain or soap bubbles in ventricles).

hySections.heading: Echinococcus granulosus
bullets: Aka hydatid worm, or dog tapeworm; causes hydatid cyst disease.
Acquired from dogs (clearly).
Causes liver cysts. Only point you need to know is that you do not biopsy because this can cause anaphylaxis. Tx = surgically remove.

hySections.heading: Schistosoma
bullets: Penetrates skin when swimming; snail is host.
Schistosoma mansoni/japonicum can cause portal hypertension. Not HY but shows up once on NBME. Not to be confused with Schistoma hematobium, which causes squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

hySections.heading: Paragonimus westermani
bullets: Ingested from crab meat or crayfish.
Aka lung fluke. Most common cause of hemoptysis in the world.

hySections.heading: Clonorchis sinensis
bullets: Ingested from fish. Causes cholangiocarcinoma.

topics.title: GI pharm
topics.summary: Omeprazole.

hySections.heading: PPIs
bullets: Omeprazole.
Shut of proton pumps on parietal cells → ↓ acid secretion.
Irreversible and non-competitive; more efficacious than H2 blockers, which are reversible and competitive.
Choose PPIs over H2 blockers for Tx of most things, like GERD, ulcers, and H. pylori.
Diagnosis of GERD is 2-week trial of PPIs.
PPIs cannot be given with sucralfate or -azole antifungals (on NBME).

hySections.heading: H2-blockers
bullets: Cimetidine, ranitidine.
Not used often. PPIs more efficacious.
Cimetidine can cause gynecomastia (HY on USMLE) and inhibits P-450.

Ranitidine doesn’t inhibit P-450. Sounds pedantic, but there’s an NBME Q where they mention coma in someone taking diazepam + 2nd drug → answer = cimetidine as 2nd drug; ranitidine also listed but wrong (doesn’t inhibit P-450).

hySections.heading: Metoclopramide
bullets: As discussed earlier, anti-emetic + prokinetic agent (means ↑ peristalsis).
D2 antagonist but also an antagonist of serotonin 5HT3 and agonist of 5HT4 receptors. The effects on serotonin receptors ↑ gut peristalsis.
HY use on USMLE is diabetic gastroparesis (i.e., sounds like GERD but patient has severe diabetes, where answer is metoclopramide, not PPI).

Because it’s a D2-antagonist, adverse effects are similar to the anti-psychotics – i.e., prolong QT interval, hyperprolactinemia, anti-pyramidal effects (acute dystonia, parkinsonism, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia).

hySections.heading: Ondansetron
bullets: Powerful anti-emetic classically used for nausea/vomiting from chemoradiotherapy.
5HT3 antagonist.

hySections.heading: Erythromycin
bullets: Motilin receptor agonist that can be used for diabetic gastroparesis.
Also a 50S ribosomal subunit inhibitor (antibiotic).

hySections.heading: Misoprostol
bullets: PGE1 analogue. Used for NSAID-induced ulcers after PPIs.
NSAIDs ↓ prostaglandins. Therefore misoprostol is the replenished prostaglandin.
Prostaglandins ↓ acid production, ↑ mucous and bicarb production, and ↑ gastric mucosal blood flow.

hySections.heading: Magnesium
bullets: Antacid. Causes diarrhea.

hySections.heading: Aluminum
bullets: Antacid. Causes constipation (“Aluminimum amount of feces.”)

hySections.heading: Calcium
bullets: Antacid. Causes milk-alkali syndrome (↑ Ca2+ + ↑ HCO3-+ renal dysfunction).

Bisphosphonates (e.g., alendronate) and tetracyclines (e.g., doxycycline) cannot be taken with calcium or iron supplements (i.e., divalent cations), since the latter chelate the drugs and ↓ absorption / oral bioavailability. USMLE loves this.

USMLE will give you, e.g., prostatitis treated with ciprofloxacin, + list all sorts of other meds the patient is on, as well as a calcium supplement, and then tell you the patient’s condition isn’t improving + ask why → answer = calcium carbonate.

hySections.heading: Bismuth
bullets: Can be used as part of H. pylori regimens (but not first-line).

hySections.heading: Sucralfate
bullets: Can be used to coat ulcers / form a barrier to protect against acid and ↓ pain.
Cannot take with PPIs. The latter ↓ ability of sucralfate to crosslink/work correctly.

hySections.heading: 5-ASA compounds
bullets: Mesalamine, sulfasalazine; NSAIDs used for IBD, as discussed earlier.

hySections.heading: TNF-a blockers
bullets: Infliximab, adalimumab, and etanercept.
USMLE likes these for IBD after 5-ASA compounds and steroids are attempted.
Infliximab and adalimumab are monoclonal antibodies against TNF-a.
Etanercept is a recombinant receptor that mops up soluble TNF-a.

hySections.heading: Propranolol
bullets: Beta-blocker that can be used for esophageal varices prophylaxis (not Tx).

hySections.heading: Lactulose
bullets: Used to Tx hyperammonemia in cirrhosis.
Carbohydrate that is metabolized by gut bacteria into acidic substrates that trap ammonia as ammonium. The latter is then excreted (ions aren’t absorbed as easily).
The answer on USMLE is “acidification, NH4+” for what lactulose causes in the gut.

hySections.heading: Neomycin
bullets: Antibiotic that kills ammonia-producing bacteria.

hySections.heading: Ezetimibe
bullets: Blocks cholesterol absorption in the small bowel.

hySections.heading: Cholestyramine
bullets: Bile acid sequestrant. Causes reduced enterohepatic circulation of bile acids at terminal ileum → liver must now convert more cholesterol into bile acids in order to replenish them → liver pulls cholesterol out of the blood to accomplish this.

hySections.heading: Orlistat
bullets: Pancreatic lipase inhibitor used for obesity; can cause steatorrhea.

hySections.heading: Nystatin
bullets: Mouth wash used for oropharyngeal candidiasis.
Forms pores in fungal ergosterol membrane.

hySections.heading: Fluconazole
bullets: Used for candidal esophagitis.
Inhibits ergosterol synthesis (i.e., lanosterol → ergosterol) by inhibiting 14a- demethylase. USMLE can write this as “P-450-mediated demethylation reaction.”

hySections.heading: Acyclovir
bullets: HSV esophagitis; HSV1/2 causes “punched out” ulcers.
DNA polymerase inhibitor; causes chain termination; resistance = altered viral thymidine kinase.

hySections.heading: Ganciclovir
bullets: CMV esophagitis and colitis; causes linear/confluent ulcers. Same MOA as acyclovir.

hySections.heading: CAP
bullets: Clarithromycin, Amoxicillin, PPI.
First-line Tx for H. pylori.
If patient still has (+) urease breath test after 4 weeks, assume antibiotics resistance and switch out the CA and add tetracycline, metronidazole, and bismuth (keep PPI).

hySections.heading: Vancomycin
bullets: Given orally to treat C. difficile.

hySections.heading: Metronidazole
bullets: “Anaerobes below the diaphragm.”
Used for diverticulitis in combo with a fluoroquinolone.
Tx for Giardia + Entamoeba.

hySections.heading: Imipenem
bullets: Carbapenem antibiotic that has fantastic penetration for pancreatitis.

hySections.heading: Mebendazole
bullets: Used for most nematodes (i.e., Ascariasis, Enterobiasis, hookworms, etc.).
Inhibits microtubules. An NBME Q has “tubulin” as the answer for protein it inhibits.

hySections.heading: Albendazole
bullets: Same as mebendazole, but for whatever reason it’s known as a preferred agent for neurocysticercosis, which is caused by a cestode (Taenia solium).

hySections.heading: Pyrantel pamoate
bullets: Agent used against nematodes. Shows up on an offline NBME as answer.
Causes paralysis.

hySections.heading: Praziquantel
bullets: Used for cestodes and trematodes.
Renal + gonadal (testicular in men; ovarian in women) arteries come off of L2 most often.
Abdominal aorta bifurcates into common iliacs at L4.
USMLE wants you to know HepB is “DNA, enveloped, circular” and has a polymerase enzyme with dual function: DNA-dependent DNA polymerase + RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (reverse transcriptase).
USMLE is obsessed with HepB serology:
USMLE wants the arrow combination (up, down, unchanged) for LES tone and peristalsis in CREST syndrome; answer = down arrow for both (this is on retired NBME 13 I think for Step 1).
Grehlin stimulates appetite (greatest when haven’t eaten for a while).
Acute pancreatitis + dyspnea + low O2 sats + bilateral infiltrates = ARDS.
Really HY point is that metoclopramide is first-line pharmacologic agent in those with diabetic gastroparesis. USMLE will slam people on how this contrasts with GERD:

Regarding gastroparesis, the USMLE vignette will make an explicit point about bad diabetic disease, i.e., peripheral edema (renal insufficiency due to decreased oncotic pressure from albuminuria) +/- cataracts (osmotic damage from intracellular sorbitol) +/- urinary retention (neurogenic bladder due to osmotic denervation leading to hypocontractile detrusor) +/- they simply say HbA1C of 12% (diabetes is 6.5% or greater; prediabetic is 6-6.49). There will be no question as to whether they want gastroparesis vs simple GERD.
Octreotide + somatostatinomas cause steatorrhea due to inhibition of pancreatic lipase secretion.
Proton pump inhibitors (e.g., omeprazole) are more efficacious than H2-blockers. PPIs are irreversible and non-competiive; H2-blockers are reversible and competitive.

Also a 50S ribosomal subunit inhibitor (antibiotic).
PGE1 analogue. Used for NSAID-induced ulcers after PPIs.
NSAIDs ↓ prostaglandins. Therefore misoprostol is the replenished prostaglandin.
Prostaglandins ↓ acid production, ↑ mucous and bicarb production, and ↑ gastric mucosal blood flow.
Antacid. Causes diarrhea.
Antacid. Causes constipation (“Aluminimum amount of feces.”)
Antacid. Causes milk-alkali syndrome (↑ Ca2+ + ↑ HCO3-+ renal dysfunction).

Bisphosphonates (e.g., alendronate) and tetracyclines (e.g., doxycycline) cannot be taken with calcium or iron supplements (i.e., divalent cations), since the latter chelate the drugs and ↓ absorption / oral bioavailability. USMLE loves this.

USMLE will give you, e.g., prostatitis treated with ciprofloxacin, + list all sorts of other meds the patient is on, as well as a calcium supplement, and then tell you the patient’s condition isn’t improving + ask why → answer = calcium carbonate.
Can be used as part of H. pylori regimens (but not first-line).
Can be used to coat ulcers / form a barrier to protect against acid and ↓ pain.
Cannot take with PPIs. The latter ↓ ability of sucralfate to crosslink/work correctly.
Mesalamine, sulfasalazine; NSAIDs used for IBD, as discussed earlier.
Infliximab, adalimumab, and etanercept.
USMLE likes these for IBD after 5-ASA compounds and steroids are attempted.
Infliximab and adalimumab are monoclonal antibodies against TNF-a.
Etanercept is a recombinant receptor that mops up soluble TNF-a.
Beta-blocker that can be used for esophageal varices prophylaxis (not Tx).
Used to Tx hyperammonemia in cirrhosis.
Carbohydrate that is metabolized by gut bacteria into acidic substrates that trap ammonia as ammonium. The latter is then excreted (ions aren’t absorbed as easily).
The answer on USMLE is “acidification, NH4+” for what lactulose causes in the gut.
Antibiotic that kills ammonia-producing bacteria.
Blocks cholesterol absorption in the small bowel.

Bile acid sequestrant. Causes reduced enterohepatic circulation of bile acids at terminal ileum → liver must now convert more cholesterol into bile acids in order to replenish them → liver pulls cholesterol out of the blood to accomplish this.
Pancreatic lipase inhibitor used for obesity; can cause steatorrhea.
Mouth wash used for oropharyngeal candidiasis.
Forms pores in fungal ergosterol membrane.
Used for candidal esophagitis.
Inhibits ergosterol synthesis (i.e., lanosterol → ergosterol) by inhibiting 14a- demethylase. USMLE can write this as “P-450-mediated demethylation reaction.”
HSV esophagitis; HSV1/2 causes “punched out” ulcers.
DNA polymerase inhibitor; causes chain termination; resistance = altered viral thymidine kinase.
CMV esophagitis and colitis; causes linear/confluent ulcers. Same MOA as acyclovir.
Clarithromycin, Amoxicillin, PPI.
First-line Tx for H. pylori.
If patient still has (+) urease breath test after 4 weeks, assume antibiotics resistance and switch out the CA and add tetracycline, metronidazole, and bismuth (keep PPI).
Given orally to treat C. difficile.
“Anaerobes below the diaphragm.”
Used for diverticulitis in combo with a fluoroquinolone.
Tx for Giardia + Entamoeba.
Carbapenem antibiotic that has fantastic penetration for pancreatitis.
Used for most nematodes (i.e., Ascariasis, Enterobiasis, hookworms, etc.).
Inhibits microtubules. An NBME Q has “tubulin” as the answer for protein it inhibits.
Same as mebendazole, but for whatever reason it’s known as a preferred agent for neurocysticercosis, which is caused by a cestode (Taenia solium).
Agent used against nematodes. Shows up on an offline NBME as answer.
Causes paralysis.
Used for cestodes and trematodes.
Renal + gonadal (testicular in men; ovarian in women) arteries come off of L2 most often.
Abdominal aorta bifurcates into common iliacs at L4.
USMLE wants you to know HepB is “DNA, enveloped, circular” and has a polymerase enzyme with dual function: DNA-dependent DNA polymerase + RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (reverse transcriptase).
USMLE is obsessed with HepB serology:
USMLE wants the arrow combination (up, down, unchanged) for LES tone and peristalsis in CREST syndrome; answer = down arrow for both (this is on retired NBME 13 I think for Step 1).
Grehlin stimulates appetite (greatest when haven’t eaten for a while).
Acute pancreatitis + dyspnea + low O2 sats + bilateral infiltrates = ARDS.
Really HY point is that metoclopramide is first-line pharmacologic agent in those with diabetic gastroparesis. USMLE will slam people on how this contrasts with GERD:

Regarding gastroparesis, the USMLE vignette will make an explicit point about bad diabetic disease, i.e., peripheral edema (renal insufficiency due to decreased oncotic pressure from albuminuria) +/- cataracts (osmotic damage from intracellular sorbitol) +/- urinary retention (neurogenic bladder due to osmotic denervation leading to hypocontractile detrusor) +/- they simply say HbA1C of 12% (diabetes is 6.5% or greater; prediabetic is 6-6.49). There will be no question as to whether they want gastroparesis vs simple GERD.
Octreotide + somatostatinomas cause steatorrhea due to inhibition of pancreatic lipase secretion.
Proton pump inhibitors (e.g., omeprazole) are more efficacious than H2-blockers. PPIs are irreversible and non-competiive; H2-blockers are reversible and competitive.

rapidFireQAs.q: 21F + stressed studying for med school exams + two-day history of yellow eyes + no other symptoms + has had a few episodes like this before. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for hematocrit, indirect bilirubin, direct bilirubin, and total bilirubin?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↔ Hematocrit, ↑ indirect bilirubin, ↔ direct bilirubin, ↑ total bilirubin. — Diagnosis is Gilbert syndrome (pronounced Jeel-BEAR). • Mechanism is decreased uptake enzyme at the liver for bilirubin (UDP-glucuronosyltransferase). • Benign condition. No treatment necessary. • Indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin = not water-soluble; type of bilirubin that exists after RBCs are broken down in the spleen, but before the bilirubin arrives at the liver. • Direct (conjugated) bilirubin = water-soluble; the type of bilirubin that exists after it is taken up by the liver and secreted into bile. • Indirect bilirubin is high in hemolysis (i.e., hemolytic anemia, spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency), sickle cell, and Gilbert syndrome. • Direct bilirubin is high if we have post-hepatic obstruction (i.e., choledocholithiasis, head of pancreas cancer impinging on common bile duct, biliary atresia), autoimmune disease (primary sclerosing cholangitis, primary biliary cirrhosis). • Some conditions can present with either conjugated or unconjugated (i.e., cirrhosis, hepatitis). • In Gilbert, hematocrit is normal because this condition has nothing to do with hemolysis or RBC turnover. • Indirect bilirubin is high because the liver cannot take up the bilirubin. • Direct bilirubin is normal because there is no post- or intra-hepatic obstruction. • Total bilirubin is increased because indirect bilirubin is high. Total bilirubin, in and of itself, does not tell us anything about etiology. We want to know whether a patient has high direct or indirect bilirubin.

rapidFireQAs.q: 57F + jaundiced + pale stools + dark urine + had cholecystectomy performed one week ago + intraoperative cholangiography was not performed. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for hematocrit, indirect bilirubin, direct bilirubin, and total bilirubin?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↔ Hematocrit, ↔ indirect bilirubin, ↑ direct bilirubin, ↑ total bilirubin. — Diagnosis is choledocholithiasis (stone in the biliary tree). • Do not confuse this with cholelithiasis, which is a stone in the gall bladder. • One of the vignettes USMLE will give is someone with recent cholecystectomy. The implication is there may have been a retained stone in the cystic duct that descended into the common bile duct post-operatively. The question need not mention intraoperative cholangiography was not performed. • Because we have a post-hepatic biliary obstruction, direct bilirubin is high. • Since less bilirubin can make its way into the small bowel, and then ultimately into the stool, stools can be pale or whiteish in appearance (known as acholic stools). • The direct bilirubin, since it is water-soluble, can make its way into the urine (dark urine). • Indirect bilirubin is normal because we have no problem with uptake, nor do we have increased breakdown of RBCs. A blockage after the liver can sometimes lead to increases in indirect bilirubin, but the classic USMLE picture for obstruction is high direct with normal indirect. • Total bilirubin is high because the direct bilirubin is elevated.

rapidFireQAs.q: 10M + recently took dapsone + yellow eyes. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for hematocrit, indirect bilirubin, direct bilirubin, and total bilirubin?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↓ Hematocrit, ↑ indirect bilirubin, ↔ direct bilirubin, ↑ total bilirubin. — Diagnosis is G6PD deficiency. Hemolysis can be precipitated by drugs such as dapsone and primaquine, as well as by fava beans. • In G6PD deficiency, there is less NADPH production, so RBCs are more prone to oxidative stress. • Since we have increased RBC breakdown and turnover, more indirect bilirubin will be produced, thereby also increasing total bilirubin. • Direct bilirubin may be normal or slightly increased. The liver has a high capacity to handle increased indirect bilirubin arriving for uptake. If you get a Q where the focus is hemolysis, you will see that the increase in bilirubin is predominantly indirect, with no change, or a very marginal increase, in direct bilirubin.

rapidFireQAs.q: 43M + treated with cimetidine for gastric ulcers. As a result of this medication, what are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for intracellular inositol triphosphate (IP3), diacylglycerol (DAG), and cAMP?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↔ IP3, ↔ DAG, ↓ cAMP. — Cimetidine is a histamine-2 receptor blocker (H2 blocker). • The H2 receptor is a G-a-s G-protein. Agonism increases cAMP. However, since cimetidine is an H2 antagonist, cAMP will decrease. • Cimetidine can cause gynecomastia (HY for USMLE). • Once again, don’t stress about the above diagram. I only put it in here because some students will flip out if I don’t. If you don’t remember any of this stuff, just know oxytocin and cimetidine, as I discussed above.

rapidFireQAs.q: Virchow node (Troisier sign)
rapidFireQAs.a: palpable supraclavicular lymph node that can reflect visceral malignancy, especially gastric cancer. Hyperbilirubinemia

rapidFireQAs.q: USMLE likes acute exacerbations of hyperammonemia caused by GI bleeds
rapidFireQAs.a: ↑ ammonia absorption.

rapidFireQAs.q: Both are associated with HLA-B27
rapidFireQAs.a: PAIR → Psoriasis, Ankylosing spondylitis, IBD, Reactive arthritis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Pain starts at epigastrium (visceral pain) and migrates toward RLQ (parietal pain). USMLE will ask why there is movement of the pain
rapidFireQAs.a: “inflammation of the parietal peritoneum.” In other words, organ pain (visceral pain) is felt somewhat non-specifically around the epigastrium. But once it becomes more superficial and involves the parietal peritoneum, it is felt more localized.

rapidFireQAs.q: USMLE wants you to know appendicitis pain can be RUQ in pregnancy due to displacement of bowel and a shift in appendiceal location. What they will do is tell you pregnant woman in 3rd trimester has RUQ pain, fever, and vomiting + negative abdo ultrasound (meaning not cholecystitis)
rapidFireQAs.a: “appendicitis.”

rapidFireQAs.q: USMLE will give ethics/consent Q, where they say patient has operation performed for ovarian procedure but it is seen that she has an acutely inflamed appendix
rapidFireQAs.a: “remove due to necessity of medical emergency.”

rapidFireQAs.q: ECG
rapidFireQAs.a: Entamoeba histolytica, Cryptosporidium parvum, and Giardia lamblia are all GI protozoa that are acquired via cysts in water (i.e., they are water-borne). If “water-borne” and “fecal-oral” are both listed as answers, USMLE wants “water-borne” as means of acquisition.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M + fasting glucose of 112 mg/dL + dark skin on forearms + arthritis; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: hereditary hemochromatosis → AR, chromosome 6, HFE gene, C282Y or H63D missense mutations account for 90% → “Bronze diabetes” → hyperpigmentation (from hemosiderin deposition) + diabetes due to iron deposition in tail of pancreas (normal fasting glucose is 72-99 mg/dL; impaired fasting glucose [pre-diabetic] is 100-125 mg/dL; diabetic is two fasting glucoses 126 or greater, or a single HbA1c >6.5%, or any random glucose >200 mg/dL) + third finding such as arthritis, cardiomyopathy, or infertility.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M + fasting glucose of 130 mg/dL + hands are sore + x-ray of hands shows DIP involvement; what’s the Dx for the type of arthritis?
rapidFireQAs.a: pseudogout, not osteoarthritis. Student says ? The two most common etiologies for pseudogout are hemochromatosis and primary hyperparathyroidism (pseudogout is calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, and will present as either a monoarthritis of a large joint such as the knee, or as an osteoarthritis-like presentation of the hands.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of hereditary hemochromatosis
rapidFireQAs.a: serial phlebotomy, not chelation therapy.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M patient above + USMLE asks what’s the mechanism for his disease
rapidFireQAs.a: “increased intestinal absorption of iron.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M above + next best step in Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: check serum ferritin (>300 ug/L in men + post-menopausal women; or >200 in premenopausal women; USMLE will always say >300 so don’t worry).

rapidFireQAs.q: Why do men get hemochromatosis younger + with worse Sx than women?
rapidFireQAs.a: menstruation slows progression of disease.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is secondary hemochromatosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: aka transfusional siderosis (amazing to remember if you want to sound sophisticated) → due to chronic blood transfusions → each transfusion of RBCs contains iron → seen classically in beta-thalassemia major or any other patients receiving ongoing transfusions.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for secondary hemochromatosis (transfusional siderosis)
rapidFireQAs.a: chelation therapy (e.g., deferoxamine), not serial phlebotomy.

rapidFireQAs.q: Three main conditions causing hepatocellular carcinoma?
rapidFireQAs.a: HepB, HepC, hemochromatosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tumor marker of HCC?
rapidFireQAs.a: AFP (same as yolk sac tumor, aka endodermal sinus tumor).

rapidFireQAs.q: Parkinsonism in young patient; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Wilson disease (AR, chromosome 13)

rapidFireQAs.q: Parkinsonism in older patient; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Parkinson disease

rapidFireQAs.q: Parkinsonism + axial dystonia; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: progressive supranuclear palsy (this is on the USMLE!!)

rapidFireQAs.q: Parkinsonism + visual hallucinations + cognitive decline; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Lewy body dementia

rapidFireQAs.q: Parkinsonism + urinary incontinence + gait instability + cognitive dysfunction; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) = “wet, wobbly, wacky” + Parkinsonism.

rapidFireQAs.q: 23F + unilateral resting tremor + increased LFTs + hemolytic anemia; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Wilson disease

rapidFireQAs.q: 23F + unilateral resting tremor + increased LFTs + hemolytic anemia; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: do a slit-lamp exam.

rapidFireQAs.q: How is most copper normally excreted by the body?
rapidFireQAs.a: through bile (hepatocyte transport pump).

rapidFireQAs.q: Important serum/blood findings in Wilson?
rapidFireQAs.a: decreased ceruloplasmin; increased urinary copper.

rapidFireQAs.q: How do we normally excrete iron?
rapidFireQAs.a: humans have poor elimination mechanism; losses are natural through skin (or menstruation in women).

rapidFireQAs.q: Where do we absorb iron and copper?
rapidFireQAs.a: duodenum mainly.

rapidFireQAs.q: Where do we absorb bile acids and B12?
rapidFireQAs.a: terminal ileum.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for Wilson disease?
rapidFireQAs.a: penicillamine (copper chelator).

rapidFireQAs.q: “Opposite” of Wilson disease?
rapidFireQAs.a: Menkes disease (can’t absorb intestinal copper).

rapidFireQAs.q: What vitamin helps absorb iron?
rapidFireQAs.a: vitamin C ferrireductase converts small bowel Fe3+ to Fe2+; only Fe2+ can be absorbed out of the lumen.

rapidFireQAs.q: What does cholecystokinin (CCK) do?
rapidFireQAs.a: increases contraction of gall bladder, relaxes sphincter of Oddi, and increases exocrine pancreas secretion of lipases, proteases, and amylase.

rapidFireQAs.q: Which cells make CCK
rapidFireQAs.a: “enteroendocrine cells of the small intestine” → HY.

rapidFireQAs.q: Macronutrients entering the duodenum (i.e., fats, proteins, carbs); what hormone is notably secreted in response?
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE wants CCK for this one.

rapidFireQAs.q: Acid entering the duodenum; what hormone is notably secreted in response?
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE wants secretin → causes bicarb secretion from pancreas.

rapidFireQAs.q: What do gastric chief cells do?
rapidFireQAs.a: secrete pepsinogen (inactive zymogen) → acid activates to pepsin.

rapidFireQAs.q: What do parietal cells secrete
rapidFireQAs.a: acid + intrinsic factor.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M + vitiligo + macrocytic anemia; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: pernicious anemia causing B12 deficiency → “autoimmune diseases go together.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism for pernicious anemia?
rapidFireQAs.a: autoantibodies against parietal cells or intrinsic factor.

rapidFireQAs.q: Blood smear in pernicious anemia?
rapidFireQAs.a: hypersegmented neutrophils + high MCV RBCs.

rapidFireQAs.q: Pt has B12 deficiency + atrophic gastritis; what is most likely to be increased in this pt?
rapidFireQAs.a: gastrin → need to assume pernicious anemia → atrophy of parietal cells due to Abs → decreased acid production → increased gastrin → USMLE likes this question!

rapidFireQAs.q: Which nerve must be severed to remove cancer at gastroesophageal junction
rapidFireQAs.a: vagus (just memorize it; it’s on a retired NBME).

rapidFireQAs.q: HY structures passing through diaphragm?
rapidFireQAs.a: “I Ate 10 Eggs At 12.” → IVC T8; T10 Esophagus + thoracic duct; Aortic hiatus (aorta, azygous vein, thoracic duct) at T12.

rapidFireQAs.q: Drug-/pill-induced esophagitis
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE wants bisphosphonates (i.e., alendronate) + tetracyclines + clindamycin as causes.

rapidFireQAs.q: What part of the brain is damaged in Wilson?
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE wants putamen (they will show you a transverse head CT and expect you to pick out the letter labeling the putamen).

rapidFireQAs.q: Most active part of the bowel in terms of cell division?
rapidFireQAs.a: “base of the crypt.” Memorize it. “Top of the villi” is the wrong answer.

rapidFireQAs.q: Where are Brunner glands
rapidFireQAs.a: duodenum, proximal to the sphincter of Oddi.

rapidFireQAs.q: What do Brunner glands secrete?
rapidFireQAs.a: alkaline mucous.

rapidFireQAs.q: What do Paneth cells secrete?
rapidFireQAs.a: Defensins in the small intestine.

rapidFireQAs.q: Person who’s vomiting; what’s the biochemical disturbance?
rapidFireQAs.a: hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis → low K, low Cl, high pH, high bicarb, low H, anion gap normal (even though it’s alkalosis, not acidosis, the USMLE will still ask an arrow for the anion gap here).

rapidFireQAs.q: 2-week-old male + forceful non-bilious vomiting; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of pyloric stenosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: abdominal ultrasound to show olive-shaped hypertrophied pylorus.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of pyloric stenosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: myomectomy

rapidFireQAs.q: Who gets pyloric stenosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: first-born males (weird, but it’s on an old NBME) + neonates taking oral erythromycin for chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum (erythromycin is a motilin-receptor agonist).

rapidFireQAs.q: 2-week-old male + bilious vomiting; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: duodenal atresia, annular pancreas, congenital midgut volvulus, or Hirschsprung (correct, Hirschsprung can present with bilious vomiting).

rapidFireQAs.q: 2-week-old + Down syndrome + bilious vomiting + passed meconium ok; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: duodenal atresia

rapidFireQAs.q: 2-week-old + Down syndrome + bilious vomiting + slow to pass meconium; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Hirschsprung

rapidFireQAs.q: How do you Dx duodenal atresia?
rapidFireQAs.a: abdominal x-ray (AXR) showing double-bubble sign (very HY).

rapidFireQAs.q: How do you Dx Hirschsprung?
rapidFireQAs.a: rectal manometry, followed by confirmatory rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism for Hirschsprung?
rapidFireQAs.a: failure of migration of neural crest cells distally to the rectum.

rapidFireQAs.q: Failure to pass meconium at birth. Most likely cause overall?
rapidFireQAs.a: cystic fibrosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 18-month-old + intermittent abdominal pain + crying + blood in stool; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: intussusception.

rapidFireQAs.q: 18-month-old + intermittent squatting + crying + FOBT positive; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: intussusception.

rapidFireQAs.q: 18-month-old + occasionally brings legs to chest + vomits + abdo mass; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: intussusception.

rapidFireQAs.q: 18-month-old + occasionally brings legs to chest + vomits + no abdo mass Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: volvulus → this is congenital midgut volvulus.

rapidFireQAs.q: Presentation sounds like intussusception but no mass
rapidFireQAs.a: congenital midgut volvulus.

rapidFireQAs.q: Cause of intussusception?
rapidFireQAs.a: >99% are in kids under age 2; caused by lymphoid hyperplasia due to viral infection (e.g., rotavirus) or recent vaccination; if in adult (usually elderly), it is caused by colorectal cancer.

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx and Tx of intussusception?
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE wants enema as the answer. Even though ultrasound can be done which shows a target sign, the USMLE always wants enema. And it can be any type. I’ve seen “air contrast enema”, “air enema,” “contrast enema” all as answers. I also had a student simply get “water-soluble contrast enema” on the exam, which means gastrografin. Barium would refer to regular contrast.

rapidFireQAs.q: For contrast swallows, when to do barium vs water-soluble (gastrografin)?
rapidFireQAs.a: barium most of the time; if at risk of aspiration, must do barium because aspiration of gastrografin will cause pneumonitis. If patient has suspected esophageal perforation, do not do barium, as that will cause mediastinitis; must do gastrografin in this case.

rapidFireQAs.q: Level of celiac trunk and main branches + what’s it supply?
rapidFireQAs.a: T12; splenic artery, common hepatic artery, left gastric artery; supplies foregut (mouth to duodenum at ampulla of Vater).

rapidFireQAs.q: Level of SMA + what’s it supply?
rapidFireQAs.a: L1; supplies midgut (duodenum at ampulla of Vater until 2/3 distal transverse colon); so for instance, the right colic and middle colic arteries come off SMA.

rapidFireQAs.q: Level of IMA + what’s it supply?
rapidFireQAs.a: L3; supplies hindgut (2/3 distal transverse colon until the pectinate line 2/3 distal on the anal canal); left colic artery comes off IMA.

rapidFireQAs.q: Abdominal aortic aneurysm occurs in males over 55 who are ever-smokers
rapidFireQAs.a: a one-off abdo ultrasound is done in this patient group.

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common locations for atherosclerosis (in descending order)
rapidFireQAs.a: abdominal aorta, coronary arteries, popliteal arteries, carotid arteries.

rapidFireQAs.q: USMLE favorite question
rapidFireQAs.a: “Which of the following is supplied by an artery of the foregut but is not itself derived from the foregut?” → answer = spleen.

rapidFireQAs.q: Short gastric arteries come off which artery?
rapidFireQAs.a: splenic.

rapidFireQAs.q: What’s the main arterial supply to the pancreas?
rapidFireQAs.a: Arteria pancreatica magna (greater pancreatic artery) → a branch of the splenic.

rapidFireQAs.q: 79M + Hx of atrial fibrillation + severe, acute, diffuse abdo pain; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: acute mesenteric ischemia caused by mural thrombus embolizing to SMA or IMA.

rapidFireQAs.q: 55F diabetic + Hx of intermittent claudication + Hx of abdo pain 1-2 hours after eating meals; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: chronic mesenteric ischemia (CMI) caused by severe atherosclerosis of SMA or IMA (essentially angina of the bowel).

rapidFireQAs.q: 55F diabetic + Hx of CABG + Hx of abdo pain 1-2 hours after eating meals; next best step in Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: mesenteric arteriography (CMI).

rapidFireQAs.q: 55F diabetic + Hx renal artery stenosis + Hx of abdo pain 1-2 hours after eating meals; Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: angioplasty + stenting (CMI) to restore blood flow.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is pectinate line?
rapidFireQAs.a: separates upper 2/3 of the anal canal (part of hindgut; endoderm-derived) from the lower 1/3 of anal canal (aka proctodeum, which is ectodermal).

rapidFireQAs.q: Lymphatic drainage above/below pectinate line?
rapidFireQAs.a: above: internal iliac; below: superficial inguinal.

rapidFireQAs.q: Arterial supply above/below pectinate line?
rapidFireQAs.a: above: superior rectal artery; below: middle/inferior rectal arteries.

rapidFireQAs.q: Venous drainage above/below pectinate line?
rapidFireQAs.a: above: superior rectal vein; below: middle/inferior rectal veins.

rapidFireQAs.q: How does pectinate line relate to hemorrhoids?
rapidFireQAs.a: above: internal hemorrhoids (painless); below: external hemorrhoids (painful).

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for hemorrhoids?
rapidFireQAs.a: conservative first, i.e., fiber + exercise; if they want intervention, banding (rubber band ligation) is the answer.

rapidFireQAs.q: How do you Dx congenital midgut volvulus?
rapidFireQAs.a: upper-GI series (AXR + contrast follow-through of esophagus, stomach, and duodenum with barium or gastrografin).

rapidFireQAs.q: What does upper vs lower GI mean?
rapidFireQAs.a: upper is above ligament of Treitz (suspensory ligament of duodenum; separates duodenum from jejunum; this ligament connects end of duodenum to the diaphragm) → below this ligament (jejunum and lower) is lower GI.

rapidFireQAs.q: Any significance to upper vs lower GI meaning?
rapidFireQAs.a: upper-GI bleeds tend to cause melena (black, tar- like stools caused by blood exposed to acid); lower-GI bleeds tend to cause hematochezia (frank blood); large upper-GI bleeds can sometimes cause hematochezia.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are the mucous-producing cells in the stomach?
rapidFireQAs.a: foveolar cells (aka surface mucous cells) secrete alkaline mucous; these are distinct from mucous neck cells, which secrete an acidic fluid containing mucin proteins.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are the mucous-producing cells in the intestines?
rapidFireQAs.a: goblet cells

rapidFireQAs.q: “Wait, so there aren’t goblet cells in the stomach?”
rapidFireQAs.a: correct.

rapidFireQAs.q: Barrett esophagus; what are the changes in mucosa (from what to what)?
rapidFireQAs.a: metaplasia of non- keratinized stratified squamous → intestinal simple columnar epithelium (intestinal means “has goblet cells”).

rapidFireQAs.q: What does Barrett look like on endoscopy?
rapidFireQAs.a: bright red mucosa (UWorld has a Q where they show the endoscopy).

rapidFireQAs.q: Barrett will go to what kind of cancer?
rapidFireQAs.a: adenocarcinoma of distal third of esophagus

rapidFireQAs.q: Biggest risk factor for Barrett?
rapidFireQAs.a: GERD (often in obese patients due to lower LES tone)

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of Barrett?
rapidFireQAs.a: PPIs are standard to decrease GERD; they’re more efficacious than H2-blockers.

rapidFireQAs.q: Acute gastritis (inflammation of lining) main causes?
rapidFireQAs.a: NSAIDs, glucocorticoids, H. pylori.

rapidFireQAs.q: Leading cause of chronic gastritis?
rapidFireQAs.a: H. pylori.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is atrophic gastritis?
rapidFireQAs.a: a type of chronic gastritis in which ongoing inflammation of glandular cells causes them to be replaced with fibrotic tissue.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is type A vs B atrophic gastritis?
rapidFireQAs.a: Type A = non-antral (mainly fundus); caused by autoimmune attack against parietal cells (pernicious anemia), resulting in B12 deficiency due to insufficient intrinsic factor production. Type B = antral; caused by H. pylori.

rapidFireQAs.q: How do you Dx H. pylori?
rapidFireQAs.a: urea breath test or stool antigen test.

rapidFireQAs.q: How do you Tx H. pylori?
rapidFireQAs.a: CAP = Clarithromycin, Amoxicillin, Proton pump inhibitor. If patient has positive urea breath test four weeks after Tx, assume resistance of Abx, so switch out the clarithromycin and amoxicillin and give metronidazole + tetracycline + bismuth instead (with the PPI).

rapidFireQAs.q: Urease, oxidase, catalase; H. pylori is positive for which ones?
rapidFireQAs.a: all three (asked in a USMLE Q, where they had different + and – combos, and the answer was all three +).

rapidFireQAs.q: What is peptic ulcer?
rapidFireQAs.a: gastric ulcer and/or duodenal ulcer.

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common cause of gastric ulcers
rapidFireQAs.a: H. pylori, then NSAIDs, then smoking.

rapidFireQAs.q: What about alcohol?
rapidFireQAs.a: EtOH doesn’t cause ulcers; it just prevents their healing.

rapidFireQAs.q: Weird causes of gastric ulcers?
rapidFireQAs.a: Cushing ulcers (head trauma → increased ACh outflow → increased M3 receptor agonism on parietal cells → increased acid secretion); Curling ulcers (sloughing of intestinal mucosa due to acute fluid losses typically seen with burns; think “Curling irons are hot.”)

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common cause of duodenal ulcers
rapidFireQAs.a: caused almost exclusively by H. pylori.

rapidFireQAs.q: What does USMLE care about relating to sucralfate?
rapidFireQAs.a: can coat the base of ulcers + protect them; activated by acidic pH, so can be inactivated in patients on antacids.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism via which H. pylori causes ulcers?
rapidFireQAs.a: secretion of proteinaceous products that damage intestinal mucosa (on USMLE Free 120 I believe).

rapidFireQAs.q: Gastrin levels in H. pylori?
rapidFireQAs.a: elevated; H. pylori causes increased acid secretion

rapidFireQAs.q: Cancer caused by H. pylori?
rapidFireQAs.a: MALT lymphoma (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma); H. pylori is considered a pre-MALT lymphoma condition, where eradication causes remission of 80% of low-grade stage 1E MALT lymphomas (confined to mucosa + submucosa).

rapidFireQAs.q: Key points about Whipple disease?
rapidFireQAs.a: caused by bacterium Tropheryma Whipplei → causes PAS- positive macrophages in the lamina propria of the small bowel (USMLE is obsessed with this detail); can cause arthritis and diarrhea. Tx = Abx (e.g., doxycycline).

rapidFireQAs.q: What is Tropical sprue?
rapidFireQAs.a: malabsorptive disease characterized by flattening of intestinal villi (similar to Celiac histo); etiology obscure/manifold but bacterial infection is accepted as one cause; Tx = Abx (e.g., doxycycline).

rapidFireQAs.q: Celiac disease important points?
rapidFireQAs.a: gluten intolerance; fluten found in wheat, oats, rye, and barley, so therefore will get Sx after eating, e.g., pasta (too easy for the vignette to mention though); causes flattening of intestinal villi on biopsy (image HY); patients often present with iron deficiency anemia (HY way to differentiate from lactose intolerance); Dx with Abs: anti-endomysial IgA (anti-gliadin IgA), anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA → after you get positive Abs in Dx of Celiac, USMLE wants duodenal biopsy to confirm (“no further studies indicated” is the wrong answer) → Tx = dietary changes to avoid gluten.

rapidFireQAs.q: “I’ve heard IgA deficiency relates somehow to Celiac. Can you explain.”
rapidFireQAs.a: Remember that “autoimmune diseases go together,” so increased risk of one means increased risk of another; the HLA associations are not super-strict → if patient has Celiac, he or she is 10-15x more likely to have IgA deficiency (which one comes first is up for debate) → because these patients are IgA deficient, they will have false-negative results on antibody screening (since Abs are IgA).

rapidFireQAs.q: Weird factoid about Celiac?
rapidFireQAs.a: increased risk of T cell lymphoma; HLA-DQ2/8 positive.

rapidFireQAs.q: What immunoglobulin is produced at Peyer patches (GALT; gut-associated lymphoid tissue)?
rapidFireQAs.a: IgA. Peyer patches contain large number of IgA-secreting B cells. IgA is a dimer connected by a J-chain.

rapidFireQAs.q: USMLE wants you to know colipase deficiency is a reason why a patient with chronic pancreatitis might not be able to digest triglycerides
rapidFireQAs.a: yes, weird and random, but I don’t know what to tell you. It’s on the NBME.

rapidFireQAs.q: What’s Zollinger-Ellison syndrome?
rapidFireQAs.a: gastrin-secreting tumor → USMLE likes “recurrent” duodenal ulcers, or the presence of any single jejunal or ileal ulcer → frequently seen as part of MEN1 (pancreas, pituitary, parathyroid).

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of ZES?
rapidFireQAs.a: check serum gastrin levels; if USMLE mentions secretin-stimulation test, it’s only because they’ll say in the vignette that “gastrin is not suppressed with secretin stimulation” as a way to tell you the Dx is ZES → secretin should normally lower gastrin levels, but they remain elevated in ZES.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of ZES?
rapidFireQAs.a: PPIs, but definitive is surgical resection of tumor.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is Menetrier disease?
rapidFireQAs.a: don’t confuse with Meniere disease; Menetrier is atrophy of parietal cells (causing achlorhydria) and hypertrophy of foveolar cells (surface mucous cells) to the extent that the inner lining of stomach resembles brain gyri; can be caused by CMV infection; Meniere disease, in contrast, is a tinnitus/vertigo syndrome caused by defective endolymphatic drainage from the inner ear.

rapidFireQAs.q: Types of stomach cancer (apart from MALT lymphoma)
rapidFireQAs.a: intestinal vs diffuse type; USMLE doesn’t ask about intestinal (it’s characterized by irregular tubular histology); diffuse = linitis plastica, which is “leather bottle” appearance of the stomach → cells contain mucin and are called signet ring cells → often associated with Virchow node (pronounced ver-cough), which is a palpable left supraclavicular lymph node → this positive node is called Troisier sign of malignancy → if gastric cancer metastasizes hematogenously to ovaries, the mets are called Krukenberg tumors → biopsy shows signet ring cells containing mucin; you’ll know it’s not mucinous cystadenocarcinoma (MC) of ovary because 1, MC isn’t the bilateral type (serous cystadenocarcinoma is), 2, MC is associated with pseudomyxoma peritonei (peritoneal infiltration by mucous from tumor), and 3, MC has a “locular,” or “loculated” appearance.

rapidFireQAs.q: High ALP + high direct bilirubin + high amylase or lipase
rapidFireQAs.a: gallstone pancreatitis = choledocholithiasis.

rapidFireQAs.q: High ALP + high direct bilirubin + high amylase or lipase + remote Hx of cholecystectomy
rapidFireQAs.a: sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (can’t be a stone cuz the gallbladder was removed ages ago).

rapidFireQAs.q: High ALP + high direct bilirubin + normal amylase or lipase in someone with recent cholecystectomy
rapidFireQAs.a: choledocholithiasis (retained stone in cystic duct that descended, but not distal to pancreatic duct entry point).

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx and Tx of choledocholithiasis
rapidFireQAs.a: ERCP.

rapidFireQAs.q: High ALP + high direct bilirubin + normal amylase or lipase in someone with remote cholecystectomy
rapidFireQAs.a: pancreatic cancer.

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of pancreatic cancer
rapidFireQAs.a: CT abdo with contrast.

rapidFireQAs.q: High ALP + high direct bilirubin + normal amylase or lipase in someone with remote cholecystectomy + CT is negative
rapidFireQAs.a: cholangiocarcinoma.

rapidFireQAs.q: High ALP + high direct bilirubin + normal amylase or lipase + diffuse pruritis + high cholesterol
rapidFireQAs.a: primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC).

rapidFireQAs.q: High ALP + high direct bilirubin + normal amylase or lipase + autoimmune disease (in pt or family)
rapidFireQAs.a: PBC.

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of PBC
rapidFireQAs.a: anti-mitochondrial Abx next best step; liver biopsy is confirmatory.

rapidFireQAs.q: Recent cholecystectomy + fever + abdo pain
rapidFireQAs.a: post-op bile leak.

rapidFireQAs.q: High ALP + high direct bilirubin + normal amylase or lipase + CT shows cystic lesion in bile duct
rapidFireQAs.a: choledochal cyst → do simple excision of cyst (cholangiocarcinoma not cystic + CT can be negative).

rapidFireQAs.q: Imaging to view liver or pancreas
rapidFireQAs.a: CT with contrast.

rapidFireQAs.q: Imaging to view gallbladder
rapidFireQAs.a: abdominal ultrasound.

rapidFireQAs.q: Imaging to view gallbladder in suspected cholecystitis only if USS negative
rapidFireQAs.a: HIDA scan.

rapidFireQAs.q: Imaging to view bile ducts
rapidFireQAs.a: ERCP or MRCP (choose ERCP > MRCP if both listed).

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M + stressed studying for exams + yellow eyes + has had a few similar episodes in the past + is otherwise healthy; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Gilbert syndrome (proncouned jeel-BEAR).

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism for Gilbert?
rapidFireQAs.a: decreased expression of glucuronosyltransferase (bilirubin conjugating enzyme) in the liver → decreased ability to take up unconjugated bilirubin at the liver → jaundice.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for Gilbert?
rapidFireQAs.a: reassurance; benign condition.

rapidFireQAs.q: How do those pathologic jaundice guidelines relate to actual USMLE Qs though?
rapidFireQAs.a: if pathologic, USMLE wants phototherapy as the Tx; if that’s insufficient, do exchange transfusion → in addition, even in adults, if you see a Q where someone’s direct bilirubin is >10% of total, that’ll be a huge clue to you that an obstructive pathology is present.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are normal bilirubin levels?
rapidFireQAs.a: 0.1 mg/dL direct; 1.0 mg/dL total.

rapidFireQAs.q: 8-day-old neonate + jaundice + direct bilirubin 14 mg/dL + total bilirubin 15 mg/dL; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: biliary atresia → super HY Dx.

rapidFireQAs.q: 8-day-old neonate + jaundice + direct bilirubin 14 mg/dL + total bilirubin 15 mg/dL; next best step in diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: straight-up liver biopsy → if positive, must do liver transplant.

rapidFireQAs.q: 8-day old neonate + jaundice + direct bilirubin 1 mg/dL + total bilirubin 20 mg/dL; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Crigler- Najjar syndrome.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism of Crigler-Najjar?
rapidFireQAs.a: absence (type I) or deficiency (type II) of glucuronyosltransferase.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of Crigler-Najjar?
rapidFireQAs.a: phenobarbital is helpful in type II (why the USMLE occasionally asks this I don’t know why); Type I does not respond to phenobarbital; plasmapheresis + phototherapy are temporizing measures; liver transplant is curative.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are Dubin-Johnson vs Rotor syndrome?
rapidFireQAs.a: never asked on the USMLE but I mention them here otherwise some students would probably spasm out → high direct bilirubin due to decreased ability to secrete it into bile → DJ has black liver; Rotor does not.

rapidFireQAs.q: Over-arching HY point about hepatitis infections for USMLE
rapidFireQAs.a: they want you to know that hepatocellular damage is due to “cytotoxic T lymphocytes,” not “viral cytopathic effects.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Hepatitis B HY points
rapidFireQAs.a: parenteral transmission; in all body fluids and can be transmitted through breastmilk, sex, and IV drug use → most common transmission is vertical at birth (through birth canal); vignettes associate HepB with China; 30% of patients with polyarteritis nodosa are HepB seropositive; HepB can also cause membranous glomerulonephritis; at birth, give HepB vaccine, followed by a second dose at 2 months, and a third dose at 6 months (apparently some vaccine schedules are saying it’s no longer given at 4 months); if mom is positive for HepB, give neonate immunoglobulin + vaccine; if mom’s status is unknown, give neonate vaccine + only give immunoglobulin if mom’s results come back positive; liver shows ground-glass appearance on biopsy → I believe a UWSA2 question for Step 1 gave an IV drug user + they showed a liver with a ground- glass appearance, and the answer was HepB; everyone selects HepC because they say, “oh wow IV drug user,” but it was HepB; HepC has a nodular appearance of the liver; both HepB and C and cause hepatocellular carcinoma.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for HepB?
rapidFireQAs.a: a variety of meds; the USMLE isn’t really fussed and won’t ask you; this is more Qbank where they may show up; but some drugs are interferon-alpha, entecavir, tenofovir, telbivudine, and lamivudine.

rapidFireQAs.q: HepC important info
rapidFireQAs.a: longest incubation period (2-26 weeks); can become chronic; parenteral transmission; transmitted by blood only; not sexually transmitted (if you spend an hour and do a comprehensive literature review yourself, you’ll learn that the transmission rate among heterosexual couples where one partner is infected is exceedingly low, i.e., on the order of 1 in 190,000 sexual contacts); if transmission occurs sexually, it is due to blood exposure; HepB, for instance, is in sexual secretions; HepC is not.

rapidFireQAs.q: Appearance of liver in HepC?
rapidFireQAs.a: nodular; in contrast, HepB → ground-glass.

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of HepC
rapidFireQAs.a: ELISA + serum HCV RNA levels.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of HepC
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE likely won’t ask you; but pegylated-interferon-alpha has the greatest chance of showing up on the exam; other drugs are daclatasvir and sofosbuvir.

rapidFireQAs.q: HepD important points
rapidFireQAs.a: called a “subviral satellite” because it depends on HepB to cause infection (i.e., without HepB, HepD exposure won’t cause infection) → what’s the best way to prevent it? → answer = simply vaccinate against HepB → three types of HepB proteins form an envelope around the HepD ssRNA → infection with HepD can occur in someone with preexisting HepB infection (superinfection) or at the same time as HepB infection (coinfection); coinfection with HepB+D carries the highest mortality rate of any of the hepatitis viruses (~20%).

rapidFireQAs.q: HepE important points
rapidFireQAs.a: fecal-oral transmission (enteral); acute disease only; classically when someone travels to India or Tibet → high mortality in pregnant women is highest yield point.

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient takes Abx for several days + has watery diarrhea; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: C. difficile (pseudomembranous colitis).

rapidFireQAs.q: Which Abx cause C. diff overgrowth?
rapidFireQAs.a: clindamycin, cephalosporins, ampicillin are highest yield.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism for C. diff infection
rapidFireQAs.a: “Ingestion of spores” is correct over “bacterial overgrowth” on the USMLE → yes, disruption of normal flora leads to C. diff overgrowth, but ingestion of spores is correct answer on NBME exam.

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of C. difficile?
rapidFireQAs.a: stool AB toxin test, not stool culture (exceedingly HY).

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of C. difficile?
rapidFireQAs.a: guidelines as of Feb 2018 say oral vancomycin first-line, not metronidazole → apparently UW is updated on this too now → note that vanc is given orally → apart from C. diff, it’s always given IV because it has terrible oral bioavailability, but in the case of C. diff, where we want the drug confined to the lumen of the colon, that makes sense.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism of colonic necrosis in C. diff colonic necrosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: “cytoskeletal disruption.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient is treated with vanc for C. diff but gets recurrence weeks later; why?
