rapidFireQAs.a: “regermination of spores.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Damage to which nerves can cause constipation?
rapidFireQAs.a: pelvic splanchnic (because these are parasympathetic, which drive bowel function) → in contrast, hypogastric nerves = sympathetic (internal anal sphincter); pudendal nerve = somatic (external anal sphincter).

rapidFireQAs.q: Hepatocellular carcinoma + peanut farmer from China; cause?
rapidFireQAs.a: aflatoxin → you don’t have to like this factoid, but it’s on the NBME.

rapidFireQAs.q: Vinyl chloride exposure + liver pathology; what’s the Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: hepatic angiosarcoma.

rapidFireQAs.q: 17M + fever + tonsillar exudates + cervical lymphadenopathy + cough + hepatomegaly; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: EBV mononucleosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Alcoholic + liver biopsy shows what?
rapidFireQAs.a: Mallory hyaline → damaged intermediate filaments.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + pan-acinar emphysema + increased LFTs; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency → inability to break down elastase in the lungs, but enzyme is synthesized in liver; also causes cirrhosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + cirrhosis + fluid wave + fever + abdo pain; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP)

rapidFireQAs.q: 69F diabetic + undergoing peritoneal dialysis + fever + abdo pain; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: SBP

rapidFireQAs.q: 8M + viral infection + pedal/periorbital edema + fluid wave + fever + abdo pain; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: SBP → minimal change disease (nephrotic syndrome) causing ascites.

rapidFireQAs.q: SBP Dx
rapidFireQAs.a: paracentesis (peritoneal aspiration; don’t confuse with periocardiocentesis) + do gram- stain + look for >250 WBCs per HPF.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for SBP
rapidFireQAs.a: ceftriaxone.

rapidFireQAs.q: Cause of spider angiomata, palmar erythema, and gynecomastia?
rapidFireQAs.a: failure of the liver to process estrogen → answer also = hyperestrogenism.

rapidFireQAs.q: Clubbing causes?
rapidFireQAs.a: pulmonary disease like CF and COBD; cardiac R→L shunts; GI disease; familial, etc. Bottom line is → just be aware GI disease can cause clubbing (i.e., IBD, Celiac, primary biliary cirrhosis).

rapidFireQAs.q: Woman 20s-50s + high cholesterol + diffuse pruritis + sister has rheumatoid arthritis; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: primary biliary cirrhosis → USMLE likes “autoimmune diseases go together” in patient (or family).

rapidFireQAs.q: How to Dx PBC?
rapidFireQAs.a: anti-mitochondrial Abs first; if positive, liver biopsy is confirmatory.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate born 32 weeks gestation + fever + abdominal distension + feeding intolerance + hematochezia; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: necrotizing enterocolitis → bowel infection in premature neonates usually <32 weeks gestation.

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of NE?
rapidFireQAs.a: abdominal x-ray (AXR) visualizing pneumatosis intestinalis (air in the bowel wall), air in the portal vein, or free air under the diaphragm.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of NE?
rapidFireQAs.a: NPO (nil per os; nothing by mouth), NG decompression, broad-spectrum Abx; if necrotic bowel, must do surgery.

rapidFireQAs.q: 49M + Hx of abdo pain after meal; now presents with sepsis + diffuse, acute abdo pain; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: ruptured viscus (duodenum).

rapidFireQAs.q: 28F + pregnant + severe, acute abdo pain + jaundice + hepatomegaly + ascites + encephalopathy; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Budd-Chiari syndrome → hepatic vein thrombosis → rare, but associated with pregnancy and malignancy.

rapidFireQAs.q: Bad type of colonic polyp/adenoma?
rapidFireQAs.a: villous + sessile characteristics are more sinister than tubular + pedunculated.

rapidFireQAs.q: Colon cancer progression?
rapidFireQAs.a: step-wise → APC → KRAS → PTEN → p53. That is highly simplified, but the point is that USMLE wants you to be aware CRC occurs as a result of many mutations in sequence.

rapidFireQAs.q: 18F + CRC in family + has hundreds or thousands of polyps on colonoscopy; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: FAP (familial adenomatous polyposis) → AD, chromosome 5, APC gene.

rapidFireQAs.q: FAP + soft tissue or bone tumors; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Gardner syndrome

rapidFireQAs.q: FAP + CNS tumors; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Turcot syndrome

rapidFireQAs.q: 18F + FAP; Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: total proctocolectomy → 100% chance of colon cancer.

rapidFireQAs.q: 20M + FAP + skull tumor; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Gardner, not Turcot → skull is bone, not CNS. Oh wow, craziness.

rapidFireQAs.q: 20M + FHx of CRC + has ten polyps seen on colonoscopy; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: HNPCC (Lynch syndrome), not FAP → FAP has hundreds or thousands of polyps on colonoscopy; HNPCC has “some polyps.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism of HNPCC?
rapidFireQAs.a: “microsatellite instability,” or “defect in mismatch repair genes” → mutations in MLH1, MSH2, PMS1.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22F + has 30 polyps on colonoscopy + mom died of endometrial cancer; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: HNPCC → Lynch syndrome associated with gyn tumors such as ovarian + endometrial, as well as other organ system tumors such as pancreas, stomach, and small bowel. Testicular + prostate very rare, but gyn common.

rapidFireQAs.q: 26F + they show you pic of spoon-shaped nail + tell you her lips have been cracked + they ask you what other symptom she might have; answer = dysphagia. Dx = Plummer-Vinson syndrome
rapidFireQAs.a: triad of iron deficiency anemia (causes koilonychia; spoon-shaped nails) + angular cheilosis (cracked corners of mouth) + esophageal webs (dysphagia).

rapidFireQAs.q: What does CREST stand for?
rapidFireQAs.a: Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasias

rapidFireQAs.q: 42M + dysphagia to solids + liquids + no other Hx; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: achalasia → inability to swallow solids + liquids together implies neurogenic etiology.

rapidFireQAs.q: 42M + EtOH Hx + dysphagia to solids that progresses to include liquids; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: esophageal cancer (SCC) → dysphagia to solids that progresses to solids + liquids = cancer until proven otherwise.

rapidFireQAs.q: HY points about esophageal cancer?
rapidFireQAs.a: adenocarcinoma is distal 1/3 and is caused by GERD (obesity → low LES tone → GERD → Barrett → adenocarcinoma); SCC is upper 2/3 of esophagus and is caused by smoking + alcohol; can also be caused by webs, burns, chemicals, and achalasia (difficult, because achalasia is LES so your thought is, “how can that cause SCC of upper 2/3?” → probably the dysphagia causes increased esophageal irritation, which then becomes the risk factor for SCC).

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism for achalasia?
rapidFireQAs.a: loss of NO-secreting neurons in myenteric plexus of LES → increased LES tone → bird’s beak appearance on contrast swallow + increased tone on esophageal manometry; cause is often idiopathic, but Chagas disease (Trypansoma cruzi) is a known infective cause (rare).

rapidFireQAs.q: So when is manometry the answer for achalasia?
rapidFireQAs.a: when they show you a pic of the bird’s beak from the barium swallow already performed, so clearly the next best step is manometry. The USMLE will sometimes show a graph of a manometry that’s been performed, and you’ll simply see that the pressure is high at the LES → hence Dx = achalasia. The confirmatory / most accurate test is biopsy of LES showing loss of neurons.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for achalasia
rapidFireQAs.a: surgery first-line (endoscopic myotomy is superior to pneumatic dilatation); if patient has high surgical risk, can use botulinum toxin as first-line therapy → if fails, dCCB or nitrates.

rapidFireQAs.q: Above 42M + Hx of GERD
rapidFireQAs.a: go straight to endoscopy as the answer (cancer, not Zenker).

rapidFireQAs.q: Location + mechanism of Zenker?
rapidFireQAs.a: false diverticulum just superior to the cricopharyngeus on the posterior pharyngeal wall → USMLE answers are “increased oropharyngeal pressure” and “cricopharyngeal muscle spasm.” They want you to know it is not a congenital weakness. Dysphagia is a risk factor because this increases oropharyngeal pressure. I’ve noticed Zenker vignettes often mention the patient is overweight, although the association is non-specific.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is Whipple triad?
rapidFireQAs.a: means insulinoma → 1) hypoglycemia, 2) Sx of hypoglycemia (diaphoresis, tachycardia, tremulousness), 3) relief of Sx with meals (or they’ll say it gets worse between meals).

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + high glucose levels + body rash; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: glucagonoma → rash is called necrolytic migratory erythema and is seen in glucagonoma.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + watery diarrhea + hypokalemia + achlorhydria; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: VIPoma, aka WDHA syndrome (Watery Diarrhea, Achlorhydria, Hypokalemia).

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + increased bowel motions + facial flushing; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: VIPoma (another presentation I saw that was harder to Dx).

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + steatorrhea + pancreatic tumor; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: somatostatinoma.

rapidFireQAs.q: Biggest risk factor pancreatic cancer?
rapidFireQAs.a: smoking

rapidFireQAs.q: Biggest risk factor for gall bladder cancer
rapidFireQAs.a: smoking

rapidFireQAs.q: 52F + 2 kids + BMI 28 + recurrent colicky epigastric pain; next best step in Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: ultrasound (cholelithiasis).

rapidFireQAs.q: Why increased risk of cholesterol stones in pregnancy?
rapidFireQAs.a: estrogen upregulates HMG-CoA reductase + progesterone slows biliary peristalsis → both of these hormonal effects are exceedingly HY.

rapidFireQAs.q: Brown pigment stones
rapidFireQAs.a: bacterial infection → bacteria deconjugate bilirubin, making it less water soluble → stone precipitation.

rapidFireQAs.q: Black pigment stones
rapidFireQAs.a: hemolytic anemia / increased RBC turnover syndromes (e.g., sickle cell).

rapidFireQAs.q: What are pigment stones composed of?
rapidFireQAs.a: calcium bilirubinate.

rapidFireQAs.q: Random vignette of sickle cell anemia; Q asks you which of the following is the patient at increased risk of + all answers seem obscure
rapidFireQAs.a: cholelithiasis → black pigment stones.

rapidFireQAs.q: USMLE Q will ask you whether high vs low cholesterol, bile acids, and phosphatidylcholine = good or bad for cholesterol stone formation?
rapidFireQAs.a: high cholesterol = bad; high bile acids = good; high phosphatidylcholine = good.

rapidFireQAs.q: Travel + watery (or brown-green) diarrhea; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Travelers diarrhea → ETEC HL/HS toxins.

rapidFireQAs.q: MOA of ETEC HL toxin?
rapidFireQAs.a: HL toxin ADP ribosylates adenylyl cyclase → increases cAMP → increases Cl secretion into small bowel lumen → Na follows Cl → water follows Na → secretory diarrhea.

rapidFireQAs.q: Which organism has same MOA as ETEC HL toxin?
rapidFireQAs.a: Cholera toxin → difference is cholera is described as “liters and liters” of high-volume stool (“rice-water stool” is buzzwordy and rarely seen); if vignette wants to describe rice-water, they’ll say “specks of mucous” in high-volume watery stool.

rapidFireQAs.q: MOA of ETEC HS toxin?
rapidFireQAs.a: ADP ribosylates guanylyl cyclase → increases cGMP → decreases Cl reabsorption from lumen → more Na stays in lumen → more water stays with Na → watery diarrhea.

rapidFireQAs.q: Which organism has same MOA as ETEC HS toxin?
rapidFireQAs.a: Yersinia enterocolitica toxin → difference is Y. enterocolitica causes bloody, not watery, diarrhea, and Y. enterocolitica also causes pseudoappendicitis in children (due to terminal ileitis / mesenteric adenitis) and arthritis in adults.

rapidFireQAs.q: Reheated fried rice + watery diarrhea; organism + mechanism?
rapidFireQAs.a: Bacillus cereus → activation of spores.

rapidFireQAs.q: Kid + bloody diarrhea + petechiae + red urine; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) caused by EHEC O157:H7 or Shigella → HUS = triad of thrombocytopenia + schistocytosis (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia) + renal insufficiency; toxin will inhibit ADAMTS13 in afferent arterioles + cause endothelial damage → platelet consumption + clumping (thrombocytopenia) → RBCs shear as they pass by the platelet clumps (schistocytosis).

rapidFireQAs.q: How does HUS contrast with TTP?
rapidFireQAs.a: TTP is caused by a mutation that results in defective ADAMTS13, or antibodies against ADAMTS13, resulting in the inability to cleave vWF multimers → platelet clumping → similar progression as HUS. One of the points of contrast is that TTP is not toxin-induced, and TTP also tends to be a pentad of the HUS findings + fever + neurologic signs.

rapidFireQAs.q: Bloody diarrhea + chicken / turtles
rapidFireQAs.a: Salmonella enteritidis / typhimurium.

rapidFireQAs.q: Chicken + bloody diarrhea + most common cause overall in the US
rapidFireQAs.a: Campylobacter jejuni

rapidFireQAs.q: Bloody diarrhea + ascending paralysis
rapidFireQAs.a: Guillain-Barre syndrome caused by Campylobacter jejuni (many vignettes for GBS will not mention recent infection; GBS can also be caused by Shigella, Salmonella, and Yersinia).

rapidFireQAs.q: Homeless shelter + diarrhea or constipation + rose spots on abdomen + prostrated (lying down in pain); Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: typhoid fever → Salmonella typhi → don’t confuse with food poisoning Salmonella strains (enteritidis + typhimurium) → the reservoir for typhoid is humans; it is not spread by chickens or turtles.

rapidFireQAs.q: Shigella vs Salmonella points
rapidFireQAs.a: Salmonella produces H2S gas, is motile, and requires many organisms to cause infection; Shigella does not produce H2S gas, is non-motile, and very few organisms cause infection; they are both oxidase-negative.

rapidFireQAs.q: Incubation period for infective diarrhea?
rapidFireQAs.a: gram-negative rods are 1-3 days (E.coli, Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia).

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for food poisoning diarrhea
rapidFireQAs.a: don’t treat majority of time → answer = “Abx increase duration of fecal excretion of organism.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Creams + custards + mayo + potato salad + vomiting 1-6 hours after meal; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: S. aureus heat- stable preformed toxin.

rapidFireQAs.q: Immunocompromised + watery diarrhea; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Cryptosporidum parvum.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for C. parvum?
rapidFireQAs.a: supportive is correct over nitazoxanide.

rapidFireQAs.q: Fresh water lake / scuba diving + floaty stools; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Giardia causing steatorrhea.

rapidFireQAs.q: Who notably gets Giardia on USMLE?
rapidFireQAs.a: IgA deficiency.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for Giardia
rapidFireQAs.a: metronidazole.

rapidFireQAs.q: Travel + bloody diarrhea + epigastric/RUQ pain; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Entamoeba histolytica + liver abscess.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for the liver abscess
rapidFireQAs.a: drain.

rapidFireQAs.q: Intestinal obstruction + rough-surfaced eggs in stool; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Ascariasis (Ascaris lumbricoides)

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for most nematodes (roundworms)
rapidFireQAs.a: mebendazole or pyrantel pamoate.

rapidFireQAs.q: Kid + perianal itching; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm).

rapidFireQAs.q: Walking on soil / beach + microcytic anemia
rapidFireQAs.a: hookworm (Ancylostoma duodenale / Necator Americanus) → USMLE will ask how you acquired hookworm, and the answer is “through your feet.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Strongyloides stercoralis; how do you acquire?
rapidFireQAs.a: through skin (“through your feet”).

rapidFireQAs.q: Pregnant woman + ring-enhancing lesions on CT + cats is not an answer; how did she acquire?
rapidFireQAs.a: pork → can also get Toxo from pork.

rapidFireQAs.q: Travel to Mexico + cystic lesion seen in lateral ventricle on CT and/or “swiss cheese” appearance of brain; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: cysticercosis Taenia solium → pork tapeworm (cestode).

rapidFireQAs.q: Travel to Mexico + muscle cysts
rapidFireQAs.a: taenia solium.

rapidFireQAs.q: Pork or bear meat + fever + myalgia + periorbital edema; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Trichinella spiralis (trichinosis) → pork nematode (in contrast pork cestode [tapeworm] is Taenia solium).

rapidFireQAs.q: Fish + high MCV; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm) causing B12 deficiency.

rapidFireQAs.q: Beef + tapeworm; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Taenia saginata.

rapidFireQAs.q: Crabmeat + hemoptysis; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Paragonimus westermani.

rapidFireQAs.q: Worm + portal hypertension; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Schistosoma mansoni / japonicum

rapidFireQAs.q: Worm + cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct cancer); Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Clonorchis sinensis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Dogs or travel + liver cysts + diarrhea; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Hydatid cyst disease → Echinococcus granulosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Rupture of gastric ulcer
rapidFireQAs.a: left shoulder pain; which structure is irritated? → answer = diaphragm.

rapidFireQAs.q: Alcoholic liver disease
rapidFireQAs.a: AST/ALT classically ~2/1 and in the low-hundreds (e.g., 250/125), but I’ve seen plenty of Qs where this is not the case (e.g., ALT is normal and AST slightly elevated); in chronic disease, enzymes can be completely normal; in contrast, if you see ALT and AST in the thousands, e.g., both are 1200 and ALT is equal to or greater than AST, think viral hepatitis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Acetaminophen toxicity
rapidFireQAs.a: metabolite called NAPQI causes necrosis; give activated charcoal acutely (apparently there’s a UW Q where this is the answer); give N-acetylcysteine otherwise to “regenerate reduced glutathione” → reduced-G has a thiol group (-SH) group.

rapidFireQAs.q: Other notable hepatotoxic drugs?
rapidFireQAs.a: RIP from the TB RIPE drugs (i.e., rifampin, INH, and pyrazinamide are hepatotoxic); statins + fibrates; antifungal -azoles + terbinafine; methotrexate; halothane; acetaminophen; those are highest yield probably.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + BMI 29 + BP 140/90 + high TGAs + low HDL + elevated fasting glucose + slightly elevated AST and ALT; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: NASH (non-alcoholic steatohepatitis) → caused by metabolic syndrome → Tx is lifestyle modification to eradicate the metabolic syndrome.

rapidFireQAs.q: Above 45F + completely normal liver enzymes; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: NASH → I’ve seen plenty of Qs where all labs values they show you are completely normal + the only thing you’re left with is, “well she’s fat / has metabolic syndrome,” and you eliminate the others to just say, “well, this is NASH.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Histo of liver showing you large-ish circular lesion + tiny circles immediately next to it; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: primary hepatocellular carcinoma → smaller lesions are satellite lesions, not mets.

rapidFireQAs.q: Histo of liver showing you cancer everywhere; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: colon cancer; bc cancer is everywhere it’s mets.

rapidFireQAs.q: Leptin causes satiety (feeling of fullness); greatest just after a meal has started
rapidFireQAs.a: sounds obvious, but they show this in graph form, and the wrong answer is immediately when you start eating.

rapidFireQAs.q: Liver disease + ascites; why the ascites?
rapidFireQAs.a: increased hydrostatic pressure (portal HTN).

rapidFireQAs.q: Liver disease + peripheral edema; why the edema?
rapidFireQAs.a: decreased oncotic pressure (decreased albumin production by the liver).

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for chronic pancreatitis
rapidFireQAs.a: give patient pancreatic enzymes → “pancrelipase” is an answer on another NBME Q, which is a mixture of pancreatic lipases, proteases, and amylases.

rapidFireQAs.q: Cause of chronic pancreatitis
rapidFireQAs.a: multiple bouts of acute pancreatitis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Major causes of pancreatitis
rapidFireQAs.a: alcohol + gallstones are major causes; hypertriglyceridemia + hypercalcemia are other known causes; may also be caused by ERCP (endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography), mumps, drugs (e.g., sulfa). Absolutely do not say “scorpion sting” without saying the other causes first or you’ll get upbraided on your surg rotation.

rapidFireQAs.q: Gallstone pancreatitis = choledocholithiasis = stone in ampulla of Vater = high ALP + high direct bilirubin + high lipase or amylase
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx + Tx = ERCP.

rapidFireQAs.q: First Tx for pancreatitis in general
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE wants triad of NPO (nil per os; nothing by mouth) + fluids + NG tube → if USMLE asks for imaging, do CT with contrast to look for fluid collections + degree of necrosis → drain fluid collections percutaneously; if pseudoabscess forms and doesn’t regress, answer = internal drainage via ERCP or EUS (endoscopic ultrasound); if frank pus (fat enzymatic necrotic pancreas) >30%, must do necrosectomy (excision of necrotic pancreas) or aggressive percutaneous drainage.

rapidFireQAs.q: 72M + fatigue + low Hct
rapidFireQAs.a: do colonoscopy; most common cause of per rectum blood loss in elderly → diverticular bleed + colorectal cancer + angiodysplasia

rapidFireQAs.q: What is angiodysplasia
rapidFireQAs.a: tortuous, superficial vessels on colonic wall that rupture + bleed → painless bleeding in elderly.

rapidFireQAs.q: Difference between diverticulosis vs diverticulitis
rapidFireQAs.a: diverticulosis is simply the presence of diverticula → 50% of the US population over age 60 has them → most commonly in sigmoid colon due to law of Laplace (decreased diameter of sigmoid means greater pressure on the wall → greater propensity for outpouching); diverticular bleed is most common cause of per rectum blood loss in elderly → they need not be inflamed; in contrast, diverticulitis is when there is inflammation of diverticula.

rapidFireQAs.q: 69M + LLQ pain + fever = diverticulitis
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx with CT with contrast of abdomen → Tx w/ Abx (metronidazole, PLUS fluoroquinolone or Augmentin; USMLE won’t ask you the exact Abx, but you should be aware that metro covers anaerobes below the diaphragm) → never do a colonoscopy on someone with suspected diverticulitis, as you may cause perforation. However, after the diverticulitis is fully treated + cleared, patient will need a follow-up colonoscopy to rule out malignancy.

rapidFireQAs.q: 12M + pic showing you perioral melanosis (sophisticated way of saying hyperpigmentation around the lips); Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome → they’ll sometimes just show you the pic and then ask what kind of colonic polyps you’ll see → answer = hamartomatous polyps

rapidFireQAs.q: They show you pic of PJS hamartomatous polyp; high cancer risk from this lesion?
rapidFireQAs.a: non- cancerous.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is IBS?
rapidFireQAs.a: Irritable bowel syndrome → classically constipation +/- diarrhea +/- other GI Sx like cramping pain or GERD-like Sx that are relieved with defecation → there are many ways to Tx IBS, such as starting with psych screen, but if the USMLE asks about meds, they like lubiprostone, which is used for constipation-predominant IBS (PGE1 analogue that causes increased Cl secretion in bowel → Na follows Cl → water follows Na → softens stool).

rapidFireQAs.q: What is IBD?
rapidFireQAs.a: IBD = inflammatory bowel disease = Crohn and ulcerative colitis (UC) collectively.

rapidFireQAs.q: HLA association with IBD?
rapidFireQAs.a: HLA-B27 → “PAIR” → Psoriasis, Ankylosing spondylitis, IBD, Reactive arthritis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Crohn GI findings?
rapidFireQAs.a: mouth to anus; classically terminal ileum; frequently intermittent bloody diarrhea if colonic involvement; skip lesions causing “string sign” on contrast studies; “cobblestone mucosa”; transmural inflammation with non-caseating granulomas; perianal fistulae; B12 + fat- soluble vitamin malabsorption.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25M + oral ulcer + bloody diarrhea; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Crohn

rapidFireQAs.q: Extra-intestinal manifestations of Crohn?
rapidFireQAs.a: classically erythema nodosum (red shins; not a rash; this is panniculitis, which is inflammation of subcutaneous fat); anterior uveitis (red eyes); oxalate nephro- / ureterolithiasis (decreased fat absorption → more binding of fat to calcium [saponification] → therefore less calcium binds to oxalate → more oxalate absorbed → oxalate stones).

rapidFireQAs.q: Any weird factoid about Crohn?
rapidFireQAs.a: sometimes patients (+) for anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae Abs

rapidFireQAs.q: How to Dx Crohn?
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE wants colonoscopy

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for Crohn?
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE wants NSAIDs (either sulfasalazine or mesalamine [5-ASA] will be listed) before steroids → use immunosuppressants late (i.e., infliximab, azathioprine, etc.).

rapidFireQAs.q: Does Crohn share anything with UC?
rapidFireQAs.a: Yes, bear in mind in real life, there is overlap between the two diseases, so don’t pigeonhole things; think of these disease-associations as propensities rather than as intransigent rules.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28M + lower back pain worse in morning and gets better throughout the day + mouth ulcer; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Crohn disease (oral involvement only) + sacroiliitis (back pain Sx of ankylosing spondylitis).

rapidFireQAs.q: 20F + bloody diarrhea + sore joints + eczematoid plaque on forehead
rapidFireQAs.a: IBD + psoriatic arthritis

rapidFireQAs.q: UC GI findings?
rapidFireQAs.a: rectum-ascending (meaning, starts at rectum and ascends; does not involve anus; Crohn of course is mouth to anus); bloody diarrhea; not transmural (mucosa + submucosa involved only; unlike Crohn); no granulomas (unlike Crohn); lead pipe appearance of colon on contrast studies (unlike “string sign” of Crohn); crypt abscesses (just memorize) → lead pipe means loss of haustra (so the colon looks smooth from the outside; this is really HY!) → USMLE might also there are “microabscesses within the crypts” on colonoscopy (meaning crypt abscesses in UC).

rapidFireQAs.q: Extra-intestinal manifestations of UC?
rapidFireQAs.a: primary sclerosing cholangitis (beaded appearance of common bile duct; can be p-ANCA positive); pyoderma gangrenosum (crater on the forearm with necrotic debris); like Crohn, is associated with anterior uveitis + HLA-B27 associations.

rapidFireQAs.q: How to Dx UC?
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE wants colonoscopy.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for UC?
rapidFireQAs.a: same as Crohn for USMLE purposes, but just be aware in severe cases colectomy is performed.

rapidFireQAs.q: 65M + intermittent bloody diarrhea + now has fever of 104F + abdominal pain + high leukocytes; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: toxic megacolon → Dx with AXR, not colonoscopy! → if you scope, patient will perforate and die → AXR will show dilated bowel (e.g., one NBME Q says “12-cm cecum”); in general, know that AXR is done when you’re looking for gas.

rapidFireQAs.q: Where do most colonic ischemic ulcers occur?
rapidFireQAs.a: watershed areas → splenic flexure (watershed of SMA and IMA) + sigmoidal-rectal junction (watershed of IMA and hypogastric artery).

rapidFireQAs.q: Ondansetron
rapidFireQAs.a: 5HT3 (serotonin) receptor antagonist → anti-emetic classically for those with malignancy / undergoing chemotherapy → for Step 1, USMLE is content with you knowing MOA for ondansetron + that it acts at the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) of the caudal medulla → you need to be able to identify this on sagittal MRI.

rapidFireQAs.q: Metoclopramide
rapidFireQAs.a: D2 receptor antagonist used as a prokinetic agent / anti-emetic → don’t up this MOA; students all the time remember that it acts at D2 receptors, but not whether it’s an antagonist or agonist → easy way to remember is based on knowing its side-effects (similar to antipsychotics!) → hyperprolactinemia + tardive dyskinesia. USMLE Step 1 also wants you to know that it prolongs the QT interval on ECG. I had a student come out of the exam saying they were asked which drug doesn’t prolong QT, and they had listed agents such as metoclopramide, azithromycin, risperidone, amitriptyline, which all CAN prolong QT.

rapidFireQAs.q: 55M + BMI of 33 + vignette doesn’t mention diabetes + 3 months burning in throat
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx = GERD → Tx? = trial of PPIs (i.e., trial of omeprazole) for two weeks → relief of Sx is consistent with GERD as the correct Dx.

rapidFireQAs.q: 55M + BMI of 33 + poorly controlled diabetes (type I or II) + 3 months of burning in throat
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx = diabetic gastroparesis, NOT GERD (woahhh crazy) → first pharm Tx = metoclopramide, not PPIs. If metoclopramide not listed, choose erythromycin (motilin receptor agonist).

rapidFireQAs.q: Ursodeoxycholic acid (Ursodiol)
rapidFireQAs.a: naturally occurring bile acid given to patients with cholesterol cholelithiasis as an alternative to cholecystectomy. On USMLE, Dx of cholelithiasis = abdominal ultrasound, followed by Tx = cholecystectomy. Ursodiol can be given to select patients but is not considered the universal next best step.

rapidFireQAs.q: Octreotide
rapidFireQAs.a: somatostatin analogue → in general, think of somatostain as a hormone that shuts of secretion of other hormones (e.g., GH, VIP); it also decreases portal blood flow → used for Tx of esophageal varices AFTER banding (endoscopic ligation) is performed; in other words, on the USMLE, choose banding for varices before octreotide; propranolol is mere prophylaxis (also decreases portal blood flow).

rapidFireQAs.q: Octreotide also can be used for carcinoid tumors by causing decreased serotonin release from tumor
rapidFireQAs.a: carcinoid tumors are usually small-bowel or appendiceal (can also be bronchial) → small blue cells + S-100 positive + neuroendocrine origin → Dx with urinary 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindole acetic acid) → symptomatic only if metastasizes to liver → diaphoresis + flushing + tachycardia + tricuspid regurg + clonus (considered UMN finding).

rapidFireQAs.q: Cyproheptadine (serotonin receptor antagonist) can also be used for carcinoid, but is classically used for serotonin syndrome instead
rapidFireQAs.a: classically drug interactions like switching to an MOAi from an SSRI without not enough time passing; can also be caused by taking St John Wort if on SSRI, or by tramadol alone → serotonin syndrome does not cause tricuspid valve lesions because it’s too acute.

rapidFireQAs.q: Aluminum (antacid)
rapidFireQAs.a: causes constipation → “Aluminimum amount of feces.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Magnesium (antacid)
rapidFireQAs.a: causes diarrhea → this actually showed up as a case on 2CS (correct, CS).

rapidFireQAs.q: Calcium carbonate (antacid)
rapidFireQAs.a: can cause rebound gastric acid hypersecretion + milk alkali syndrome → hypercalcemia + metabolic alkalosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Orlistat
rapidFireQAs.a: pancreatic lipase inhibitor used in some patients for weight loss → could theoretically cause fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption due to decreased intestinal fat absorption → for USMLE simply know the MOA and that the drug exists.

rapidFireQAs.q: Loperamide
rapidFireQAs.a: mu-opiod receptor agonist used in the Tx of diarrhea → NBME exam asks this drug as an arrow question → addictive potential LOW (DOWN arrow) → because it can be used in the Tx of diarrhea, it can also therefore theoretically cause constipation (not rocket science).

rapidFireQAs.q: Lactulose
rapidFireQAs.a: used to Tx hepatic encephalopathy by decreasing serum NH3 → undigestible carbohydrate that gut bacteria convert to acidic end-product → intraluminal NH3 (absorbable) produced by bacteria is converted to NH4+ (not absorbable) → USMLE Q will ask you whether the drug makes gut conditions more or less acidic, as well as whether it’s NH3 or NH4+ that’s not absorbed (they give you different combos) → answer = “acidic; decreased NH4+ absorption.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Neomycin
rapidFireQAs.a: used to Tx hepatic encephalopathy by killing NH3-producing bacteria in the gut; USMLE will give you a big, rambling paragraph on hepatic encephalopathy and simply tell you this drug is given then ask for MOA → answer = “kills intraluminal gut bacteria.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Three mechanisms for stomach acid secretion are 1, ACh binding directly to M3 receptors on parietal cells (Vagus activity), 2, gastrin binding directly to gastrin receptors on parietal cells, and 3, gastrin causes enterochromaffin-like cells secrete histamine, which then binds to H2 receptors on parietal cells
rapidFireQAs.a: these three effects are synergistic → USMLE, in contrast, wants “permissive” for the effects of cortisol on catecholamines (cortisol upregulates alpha-1 receptors so NE + E can bind and do their job), and “additive” for the effects of anti-platelet agents used together.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is Dumping syndrome?
rapidFireQAs.a: caused by gastric bypass surgery, diabetes, or malfunctioning pyloric sphincter, in which stomach contents following a meal enter the duodenum too quickly; there are two types: early vs late → both show up in vignettes (without people even realizing they’re seeing a Dumping syndrome Q).

rapidFireQAs.q: Early Dumping syndrome
rapidFireQAs.a: 10-30 minutes after a meal → rapid entry of hyperosmolar gastric contents into duodenum → osmotic expansion of small bowel lumen → diarrhea + bloating → on USMLE, answer = “rapid emptying of hyperosomlar chyme into small bowel.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Late Dumping syndrome
rapidFireQAs.a: 1-2 hours after meal → rapid absorption of carbohydrates through small bowel wall → hyperglycemia → pancreas secretes lots of insulin → rebound hypoglycemia → USMLE merely wants you to identify this in a vignette as Dumping syndrome. They might say Hx of gastric bypass + now there’s a meal + patient gets diarrhea +/- hypoglycemia → Dx simply = Dumping syndrome.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is Blind loop syndrome?
rapidFireQAs.a: disturbance of normal floral balance in the small bowel due to disruption of peristalsis (i.e., surgery / post-surgical ileus), but may also be caused by conditions like IBD and scleroderma → leads to steatorrhea + B12 def + fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies → USMLE merely wants you to be able to make the diagnosis from a vignette → Tx is with antibiotics (doxycycline or fidaxomicin).

rapidFireQAs.q: Important points about intestinal transporters?
rapidFireQAs.a: apical = side of intestinal lumen; basolateral = side of blood; SGLT-1 are GLUT5 are apical transporters that take in monosaccharides from small bowel lumen; GLUT5 takes in fructose; SGLT1 takes in glucose + galactose (think 5 for fructose being a pentose, so SGLT1 is for the hexoses, glucose + galactose). Once the monosaccharides are in the enterocyte (small bowel cell), GLUT2 on the basolateral membrane takes them into the blood.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + exquisitely painful anal verge + refuses rectal exam; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: anal fissure.

rapidFireQAs.q: Where do anal fissures occurs?
rapidFireQAs.a: posterior in the midline, below the pectinate line.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for anal fissure?
rapidFireQAs.a: Sitz bath

rapidFireQAs.q: Acanthocytes on blood smear; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: abetalipoproteinemia or liver disease → USMLE loves heat stroke as cause of acanthocytes → 82F found unconscious on summer day + body temperature of 107F + blood smear shows acanthocytes; Dx = liver failure (heat stroke) → heat stroke = end-organ damage due to hyperthermia; heat exhaustion is hyperthermia + mental status change + fatigue + no end-organ signs.

rapidFireQAs.q: 8M + bloody stool + perfectly healthy otherwise; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Meckel diverticulum; student says, “huh, I thought that was age 2.” I agree with you. But there’s an NBME Q where the kid was 8, and the answer was Meckel → bleeding due to “heterotopic gastric / pancreatic tissue.”

rapidFireQAs.q: How to Dx Meckel diverticulum?
rapidFireQAs.a: Meckel scan (Tc99 uptake scan that localizes to diverticulum).

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for Meckel
rapidFireQAs.a: if asymptomatic, can leave alone; if symptomatic, surgical removal.

rapidFireQAs.q: Meckel diverticulum (true or false diverticulum?)
rapidFireQAs.a: true → contains all layers of bowel → mucosa + submucosa + muscularis propria + adventitia; in contrast, false (Zenker) is just mucosa + submucosa.

rapidFireQAs.q: 16F + fever + high leukocytes + RLQ pain that migrated from epigastrium; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: appendicitis (easy, but so HY how can I not at least mention it classically) → USMLE wants you to know that migration is because, initially, epigastric pain = visceral pain; RLQ pain = inflammation of parietal peritoneum. Must do a pregnancy test if female + adnexal ultrasound to look for gyn causes, i.e., ruptured cyst, etc. If male, go straight to laparoscopy. If rule out gyn cause in female, do laparoscopic removal. Ultrasound + CT can be done, but false-negatives have led to rupture + death, so they don’t change management if clinical suspicion is high, which is why pt goes straight to laparoscopy if under high suspicion for appendicitis → if during surgery the appendix is normal, answer = still remove it.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mallory-Weiss tear vs esophageal varices HY point
rapidFireQAs.a: MWT usually caused by vomiting/retching in alcoholic + presents with a little bit of blood in the vomitus; varices present with LOTS of blood → about half of patients with ruptured varix die.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mallory-Weiss tear vs Boerhaave
rapidFireQAs.a: MWT is not transmural; Boerhaave is transmural → causes subcutaneous emphysema (crepitus due to air under the skin).

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of varix?
rapidFireQAs.a: banding + octreotide.

rapidFireQAs.q: Prophylaxis for varix?
rapidFireQAs.a: propranolol. HY GASTRO

rapidFireQAs.q: Bloody diarrhea + appendicitis-like pain (pseudoappendicitis) in a child
rapidFireQAs.a: Yersinia enterocolitica

rapidFireQAs.q: Parkinsonism in young patient
rapidFireQAs.a: Wilson disease till proven otherwise

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for hereditary hemochromatosis
rapidFireQAs.a: serial phlebotomy

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for secondary hemochromatosis (transfusional siderosis)
rapidFireQAs.a: chelation therapy (deferoxamine)

rapidFireQAs.q: Colon cancer in first-degree relative (sibling or parent)
rapidFireQAs.a: start at age 40 or ten years before diagnosis in relative, whichever is earlier, and do every 5 years.

rapidFireQAs.q: Dysphagia to solids and liquids at the same time to start
rapidFireQAs.a: says neurogenic cause → achalasia

rapidFireQAs.q: Dysphagia to solids that progresses to solids and liquids
rapidFireQAs.a: esophageal cancer

rapidFireQAs.q: Halitosis +/- gurgling sound when swallowing +/- regurgitation of undigested food
rapidFireQAs.a: Zenker

rapidFireQAs.q: Zenker + achalasia initial Dx modality
rapidFireQAs.a: barium swallow

rapidFireQAs.q: After barium swallow is done and shows bird’s beak appearance
rapidFireQAs.a: monometry to confirm Dx of achalasia

rapidFireQAs.q: Pt with Hx of GERD + dysphagia
rapidFireQAs.a: straight to endoscopy to rule out cancer

rapidFireQAs.q: Diabetic pt with new-onset GERD
rapidFireQAs.a: diabetic gastroparesis

rapidFireQAs.q: Diabetic pt with new-onset GERD
rapidFireQAs.a: give metoclopramide, not PPI

rapidFireQAs.q: Cholelithiasis
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx with abdo ultrasound; fat, forties, female, fertile

rapidFireQAs.q: Biliary colic + fever
rapidFireQAs.a: cholecystitis

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of cholelithiasis + cholecytitis
rapidFireQAs.a: cholecystectomy

rapidFireQAs.q: Abdo USS negative in suspected cholecystitis
rapidFireQAs.a: HIDA scan

rapidFireQAs.q: Gall bladder doesn’t light up on HIDA scan
rapidFireQAs.a: confirms cholecystitis

rapidFireQAs.q: Cholelithiasis in pregnancy
rapidFireQAs.a: estrogen upregulates HMG-CoA reductase + progesterone slows biliary peristalsis

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of pancreatic cancer
rapidFireQAs.a: CT abdo with contrast High ALP + high direct bilirubin + normal amylase or lipase in someone with remote cholecystectomy + CT is

rapidFireQAs.q: High ALP + high direct bilirubin + normal amylase or lipase + CT shows cystic lesion in bile duct
rapidFireQAs.a: choledochal

rapidFireQAs.q: Odynophagia (painful swallowing) in immunocompromised pt
rapidFireQAs.a: esophageal candidiasis till proven otherwise

rapidFireQAs.q: Circular lesion in pancreas seen in pancreatitis
rapidFireQAs.a: pseudoabscess → answer = ERCP to drain internally

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + dark skin on forearms + increased fasting glucose; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: hemochromatosis (bronze diabetes)

rapidFireQAs.q: 25F + intermittent bloody diarrhea for 3 months + intermittent fever + weight loss
rapidFireQAs.a: answer IBD (Crohn or UC)

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for Crohn + UC
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE wants oral sulfasalazine (or mesalamine) first before oral steroids; for perianal disease in Crohn, topical agents / enemas can be used; NBME won’t make you pick between oral and topical distinguish (that’s more Qbank being pedantic); surgery can be done for UC

rapidFireQAs.q: UC + high bilirubin + high ALP
rapidFireQAs.a: primary sclerosing cholangitis

rapidFireQAs.q: Biopsy of small bowel in Celiac
rapidFireQAs.a: flattening of intestinal villi

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of Celiac
rapidFireQAs.a: IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase, anti-gliadin (aka anti-endomysial)

rapidFireQAs.q: After Celiac Ab positivity, what’s the next best step (no further intervention necessary or duodenal biopsy)
rapidFireQAs.a: duodenal biopsy (sounds wrong, but it’s what USMLE wants)

rapidFireQAs.q: Vague vignette where it sounds like either Celiac or lactose intolerance but it’s in a young adult who’s had zero symptoms until now
rapidFireQAs.a: lactose intolerance (can be adult-onset)

rapidFireQAs.q: PAS-positive macrophages in the lamina propria + arthritis
rapidFireQAs.a: Whipple disease

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for Wilson disease
rapidFireQAs.a: penicillamine

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for secondary hemochromatosis (transfusional siderosis) due to chronic blood transfusions
rapidFireQAs.a: chelation therapy

rapidFireQAs.q: Blood transfusion + fever + chills + flank pain + hypotension
rapidFireQAs.a: ABO mismatch (and positive Coombs) Decreased hemoglobin + increased bilirubin 2-4 weeks after blood transfusion; Dx? → delayed transfusion reaction → caused by the presence of recipient “amnestic” antibodies (weird, but just memorize it)

rapidFireQAs.q: 6M + hyperpigmentation around the lips + colonic polyps; what kind of polyps are they?
rapidFireQAs.a: hamartomatous; Dx = Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, characterized by perioral melanosis + hamartomatous colonic polyps.

rapidFireQAs.q: 80F + colonic diverticula; which part of the colon most likely has the diverticula?
rapidFireQAs.a: sigmoid colon.

rapidFireQAs.q: 46M + esophageal varices; which vein is most likely to have increased blood flow?
rapidFireQAs.a: left gastric vein; ↑ portal venous pressure causes backup to left gastric vein, which backs up to esophageal veins.

rapidFireQAs.q: 52M + 3-month-Hx of burning in esophagus + Hx of diabetes + ↓ pin-prick discrimination up to ankles + HbA1c of 9.6%; what’s the MOA of the most appropriate pharmacologic therapy? → answer = antagonism of D2 receptors; drug is metoclopramide; Dx is diabetic gastroparesis; metoclopramide is both a pro-kinetic and anti-emetic.
rapidFireQAs.a: In contrast, if vignette is simply 42M + GERD-like presentation + no mention of poor diabetic control, answer is “trial of PPIs” or “trial of H2 blockers” (I’ve seen both as correct answers, but if you’re forced to choose between the two, always choose PPIs) for GERD.

rapidFireQAs.q: 49M + long history of alcoholism + presents with smelly stools + pancreatic enzymes are normal; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: chronic pancreatitis → exocrine pancreas insufficiency due to repeated bouts of acute pancreatitis; pancreatic enzymes low or low-normal; steatorrhea from lack of lipases in pancreatic secretions; Tx with pancrelipase.

rapidFireQAs.q: 49M + alcoholism + had pancreatitis a week ago and recovered well with bedrest; now has fever + leukocytosis + increased serum lipase and amylase; diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: pseudocyst; this is a common complication of acute pancreatitis; called a pseudocyst because it doesn’t have actual walls; the pancreatic parenchyma encases the fluid collection; can be drained internally via ERCP.

rapidFireQAs.q: 30M + rheumatoid arthritis + overdosed on methotrexate in suicide attempt + now has massive hepatonecrosis; the liver can regenerate via which of the following cellular mechanisms?
rapidFireQAs.a: recruitment of cells from G0 into cell cycle; when there is hepatocellular damage, remaining cells in G0 (quiescent phase) will enter G1 of the cell cycle and begin replication; the wrong answer is stem cells entering G1 of cell cycle; this is because stem cells aren’t activated into G1; it is merely the case that other hepatocytes exist in G0, not undergoing replication, and are then stimulated into G1 for replication.

rapidFireQAs.q: 53M + cirrhosis + blood in stool + no pain; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: internal hemorrhoids (painless; external are painful); risk factor is increased venous pressure in superior rectal veins from cirrhosis (for external hemorrhoids choose inferior rectal veins); other important risk factor is third trimester of pregnancy.

rapidFireQAs.q: 53M + cirrhosis + vomiting copious blood; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: ruptured esophageal varices; risk factor is increased pressure in left gastric vein due to cirrhosis (esophageal veins feed into left gastric, which feeds into portal). Mallory-Weiss tears due to alcoholism with retching/vomiting often present with “just a little blood”; classically, varices = lots of blood. This isn’t a 100% rule, but it’s usually the case that varices = lots of blood; MW tear = little blood.

rapidFireQAs.q: 55M + obese + gurgling sounds when swallowing + sometimes regurgitates undigested food + halitosis; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: Zenker; risk factor is obesity; can also be seen in setting of dysphagia (e.g., from stroke Hx) due to increased oropharyngeal pressure → increased risk of outpouching.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28F + spoon-shaped nails + chapped lips + trouble swallowing; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: Plummer-Vinson syndrome; risk factor is iron deficiency anemia. PV syndrome is triad of 1) iron deficiency anemia (can present as koilonychia), 2) angular cheilitis, and 3) esophageal webs (dysphagia).

rapidFireQAs.q: 40M + Hx of GERD + new-onset dysphagia; Dx + risk factor? → adenocarcinoma of esophagus; GERD / Barrett is major risk factor; do immediate endoscopy.
rapidFireQAs.a: In short, do immediate endoscopy on USMLE to look for esophageal cancer in any patient with new-onset dysphagia who has Hx of GERD or heavy smoking/alcohol. Progression of dysphagia from solids only to solids + liquids is HY for cancer. Dysphagia to solids + liquids from the start suggests neurogenic etiology (achalasia).

rapidFireQAs.q: 65M + long-standing diabetes + new-onset GERD; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: diabetic gastroparesis; do endoscopy first to rule out physical obstruction, followed by gastric-emptying scintigraphy to diagnose; can give metoclopramide and/or erythromycin (motilin receptor agonist) to Tx.

rapidFireQAs.q: 30F + pregnant + severe epigastric pain after meals starting during third-trimester; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: cholelithiasis; progesterone slows biliary peristalsis (causing biliary sludge) + estrogen upregulates HMG-CoA reductase (increasing cholesterol concentration within bile).

rapidFireQAs.q: 2M + recent viral infection + now has intermittent vomiting and crying with blood in the stool; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: intussusception; risk factor is recent viral infection; can cause adenitis of bowel leading to telescoping; almost all intussusceptions occur under age 2; if elderly, can be colorectal cancer.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate + duodenal atresia and/or Hirschsprung; risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: –> Down syndrome is HY cause of these two findings.

rapidFireQAs.q: 4M + low Hb + Hx of diarrhea after meals; Dx + risk factor for the anemia?
rapidFireQAs.a: Celiac disease; major risk factor for anemia in peds (flattening of villi causes impaired iron absorption in duodenum.
